sens: To cover with a vault
To enclose or delimit a space
To form an arch structure
H7000.detail:
1. To cover with a vault: this means constructing a curved ceiling above a space, like an arch. In Ezekiel 46:22, it refers to the four corners of the temple courtyard, each of which is 'vaulted' — that is, covered with an arched structure that closes it from above.
2. To enclose or delimit a space: the verb describes how a vault imprisons or confines a place by covering it. This enclosure by a stone or wood structure creates a closed and protected space.
3. To form an arch structure: the action of bending or joining stones and beams to create this characteristic form of the Eastern building, solid and durable.
H7000.origine: The Hebrew verb קָטַר (qatal) expresses the idea of closing, surrounding, or joining elements to form a closed unit. The root suggests an action of construction or assembly that results in the enclosure of a space. The word belongs to the technical vocabulary of sacred architecture of the temple.
H7000.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 46:22. This passage describes the dimensions and structure of the vaulted courtyards located at the four corners of the temple courtyard, in the vision of the restored Jerusalem that Ezekiel contemplates. The context is that of the temple architecture and the meticulous description of its proportions and construction details, confirming that it is a technical building term.
H7000.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not disregard the concrete and architectural details of the temple. These vaulted courtyards are parts of God's intended dwelling; their careful construction expresses the respect and beauty that should be brought to the house of God. For the believer, this emphasizes that even the most ordinary sacred spaces are thoughtfully and wisely structured.

sens: Physical joint connecting two bones or parts of the body
Enigma or difficult problem to solve
Difficulty or doubt that troubles the mind
H7001.detail:
1. The joint is the place where two bones meet and articulate: it is the point of connection in the body. Daniel 5:6 describes how King Nebuchadnezzar, seized with fear at the sight of the mysterious hand writing on the wall, feels his joints loosen — his knees tremble and his strength leaves him, as if his body were unbinding.

2. A joint in a figurative sense is a question or enigma that poses difficulty — something whose elements are knotted, intertwined, and need to be unraveled. When Daniel 5:12 and 5:16 speak of the ability to 'solve difficult questions,' they refer to the faculty of undoing these knots, clarifying what was tangled: the king expects Daniel to read and explain the mysterious inscription engraved on the palace wall.
H7001.origine: The Hebrew word qétar literally means 'knot' or 'link.' It comes from a root that evokes the idea of tying, attaching together. In the Greek Old Testament, this word most often translates the image of the knotted and bound: a joint of the body is what holds together, and a difficult question is a knot that binds and hinders the mind until it is untied. This is why the word is used for both the physical and the mental or enigmatic.
H7001.emploi: The word qétar appears three times in the Bible, only in Isaiah 5 (Vulgate) and especially in the book of Daniel in chapter 5. In Daniel 5:6, it refers to the joints of the king's body, which loosen under the shock of fear. In Daniel 5:12 and 5:16, it takes on a more abstract meaning: it refers to questions, enigmas, or thorny problems — precisely this mysterious inscription that only Daniel can read and interpret. The passage shows how the same word expresses both physical loosening and mental inability to unravel what is knotted: the king is troubled both in body and mind.
H7001.portee: This word reminds us that fear paralyzes both body and mind, and that divine enigmas — the mysteries that God places in our path — require not our own strength, but the wisdom that only God can grant. Daniel, filled with the Spirit of God, can 'solve' what the king cannot untie: it is an image of the believer's dependence on God to understand His purposes.

sens: Aromatic perfume burned as a religious offering
That which rises, ascends to heaven
That which is pleasing to God, that which He accepts
H7002.detail:
1. Incense is a precious perfume that is burned during worship to honor God. In Jeremiah 44:21, the Judeans and their ancestors burned incense in the cities and streets, showing that it was a common and visible practice in the religious life of Israel.
2. The word evokes that which rises: the smoke of the incense ascends to heaven, symbolizing that the offering, prayer, or worship rises to God. It is a very strong biblical image: the rising perfume represents what pleases God.
3. By extension, incense figures what is pleasing to God, what is acceptable to Him. The verse from Jeremiah shows that God has not forgotten this burned incense — He has had it 'in mind,' meaning He has kept it in remembrance, He has been aware of it, and He responds to it.
H7002.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means 'to burn, to make smoke.' Incense, in all of the ancient East, was a precious substance (fragrant resin) that was burned to honor the gods. In Israel, it became a central element of temple worship, associated with prayer and spiritual offering.
H7002.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 44:21. The context is that of a prophetic confrontation: the prophet reproaches the Judeans and their ancestors for having burned incense, not only to God but also to other deities (the 'queen of heaven'). God reminds them that this incense, He has had it in mind — He has not forgotten their unfaithfulness. This passage shows that incense was a visible and memorable practice, of which God was perfectly aware.
H7002.portee: Incense reminds us that God sees and remembers our acts of worship and devotion. Nothing we offer to the Lord escapes His attention. Conversely, God is also aware of our religious waywardness. This passage invites the believer to offer to God alone sincere and exclusive worship, knowing that He is fully aware of it.

sens: City in the territory of Zebulun
H7003.detail: Kitron is a city in the territory that was allocated to the tribe of Zebulun during the division of the promised land. At the time of the conquest, the Israelites were unable to completely drive out the Canaanite inhabitants, who continued to live there under tribute to the Israelites (Judges 1:30).
H7003.origine: The name Kitron means 'incense' in Hebrew, possibly evoking a resource or characteristic of this locality. It is a geographical name from ancient Palestine, attested only once in the Bible.
H7003.emploi: Kitron appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 1:30, in the passage that lists the Canaanite cities that the Israelite tribes did not completely conquer. It is mentioned alongside Nahalol, also in the territory of Zebulun, as an example of the strongholds where the Canaanites maintained themselves despite the Israelite presence.

sens: Fragrant substance that is burned to produce aromatic smoke
Aromatic smoke that rises from a burnt sacrifice
The offering itself presented to the Lord by this smoke
Figuratively, prayer or praise ascending to God
H7004.detail:
1. Incense is a substance made from aromatic spices and resins that is burned. The Bible mentions its preparation with several ingredients (Exodus 30:35) and speaks of "anointing oil and fragrant incense" (Exodus 25:6). It is a precious material that was offered as a gift.
2. When incense is set on fire, it burns and produces a pleasant smoke. At the altar, the priest was to "burn fragrant incense" (Exodus 30:7-8), which filled the sanctuary with a sweet aroma rising to heaven.
3. The very act of burning incense constitutes an offering to God. This is why Nadab and Abihu sinned by presenting "strange fire" with incense that God had not commanded (Leviticus 10:1).
4. The Bible uses incense as an image: prayer is compared to a cloud of incense that rises before the Lord, as evidenced in Revelation, echoing Psalm 141:2 where it says, "Let my prayer rise before you like incense."
H7004.origine: The Hebrew word קְטֹרֶת comes from a root meaning "to smoke" or "to give off a scent." The same root appears in "savor of sacrifice" and describes the transformation of what burns into an invisible essence that ascends. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this word is rendered as θυμίαμα (thumiama), which becomes central in the New Testament to express spiritual offering.
H7004.emploi: The word appears 58 times, mostly in the books of the Law and Chronicles. Incense is included in the instructions for the Tabernacle: an altar of incense is required (Exodus 30:1), special wood for burning it, and specific ingredients (Exodus 30:35). The priests burned incense morning and evening (Exodus 30:7-8) as a regular act of worship. The dramatic event of the 250 men offering "incense" in rebellion against Moses (Numbers 16:17-18) shows that incense was reserved only for priests authorized by the Lord. It also symbolizes prayer: "Let my prayer rise before you like incense" (Psalm 141:2).
H7004.portee: Incense teaches the believer that worship must be pleasing to God, offered with the best one has and according to His precise instructions. It serves as a reminder that prayer and praise, like this fragrant smoke, truly ascend to the Lord and please Him. Finally, incense reveals that God desires to receive a deliberate, conscious offering, not a distracted or disorderly obedience.

sens: City of the tribe of Zebulun in the Promised Land
H7005.detail: Katthath is a city belonging to the territory of Zebulun, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. It appears in the list of cities assigned to Zebulun during the division of the Promised Land (Joshua 19:15). It is a minor locality, mentioned in passing among other cities in the same region.
H7005.origine: The name Katthath literally means "small" in Hebrew, which likely reflects the modest importance of this locality. The Bible also notes that Katthath had another name, Kitron (קִטְרוֹן), thus using two designations for the same place.
H7005.emploi: Katthath is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:15, in the context of the land distribution among the tribes of Israel during the conquest of Canaan. It is listed among the twelve cities assigned to the tribe of Zebulun, alongside Nahalal, Shimron, and other places in the same district. Its unique appearance in the Scriptures indicates that it was a small locality with no major events reported.

sens: To expel from the mouth what is in the stomach
To spit out, to expel with disgust
Figuratively: to reject, to push away violently
H7006.detail: 1. The word refers to the physical act of vomiting, violently rejecting the contents of the stomach through the mouth. It is a crude image, that of the body revolting. In Jeremiah 25:27, the drunken Judeans who "will vomit" represent a people crushed by divine judgment, disoriented and humiliated. 2. By extension, it means to spit out or expel something with disgust or repulsion, as if one cannot keep it inside. 3. Figuratively, it means to reject forcefully and violently, to push away what one abhors — an image of judgment that expels evil.
H7006.origine: The Hebrew verb קָיָה (qayah) has its root in the idea of rejection and expulsion. It is related to words expressing disgust and repulsion. The Hebrew biblical context uses this verb to express both the physical phenomenon and the theological idea of divine rejection.
H7006.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah 25:27. The Lord commands the prophet to make the kings of the nations drink a cup of wine from His wrath, and Judah will drink it too. After becoming drunk and vomiting, the people will fall without getting up, defeated by divine judgment. The image unites physical humiliation and military annihilation: vomiting is the visible sign of the total collapse of one who refuses to obey God.
H7006.portee: This raw, almost shocking word reminds us that God's judgment is not abstract: it touches the body and honor. For the reader, it emphasizes that rejecting the word of God leads to humiliation and ruin. The image remains unforgettable: it shows the cost of refusing to listen.

sens: the warm season of the year, between spring and autumn
H7007.detail: 1. Summer is the warm and dry season that follows spring. In Daniel 2:35, the prophet describes how the statue from Nebuchadnezzar's dream is reduced to dust, "blown away by the wind like the chaff of summer" — an image of emptiness and fragility. This mention of summer refers to the harvest, the time when crops are threshed and grain is separated from chaff, illustrating how earthly kingdoms are swept away in the face of the eternity of God's empire.
H7007.origine: The Aramaic word קַיִט (qayit) comes from the Hebrew verb קִיץ (qits), which means literally "to pass the summer." It is a key word in the climate of the Near East: summer is the quintessential dry season, crucial for harvests and agricultural life. The corresponding Hebrew word קַיִץ (qayits) appears elsewhere in the Old Testament with the same meaning and symbolic importance.
H7007.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Aramaic, in Daniel's speech to King Nebuchadnezzar in 539 BC. This unique presence marks a key moment: as the prophet interprets the prophetic dream, he uses the image of the summer harvest to describe the destruction of the empires of the world. Summer, a season of maturity and transition, symbolizes here both the fulfillment and the vanity of earthly powers in the face of God's eternal reign.
H7007.portee: This image of summer and the chaff blown away by the wind reminds the reader that human kingdoms, despite their apparent solidity, are as fragile as the dust of a harvest. It invites one to place their trust not in the visible powers of the world, but in the God whose reign is unshakeable and eternal.

sens: Visible emanation that rises from a fire or a source of heat
Fog or vapor floating in the air
H7008.detail:
1. Smoke is primarily what visibly rises from a fire or flame: in Genesis 19:28, Abraham sees rising from the earth "a smoke, like the smoke of a furnace" above the ruins of Sodom and Gomorrah — a striking image of destruction and divine power.
2. The word also more broadly refers to a vapor or fog that floats in the air and obscures vision. In Psalms 148:8, the "clouds" (the same word) are among the powers of nature that obey God's commands, alongside fire and hail. In Psalms 119:83, the psalmist compares himself to "a wineskin in smoke": an image of dryness and suffering, where smoke represents a hostile and suffocating environment.
H7008.origine: The Hebrew word קִיטוֹר (qitor) comes from a root that evokes the idea of rising, spiraling upward. It is related to other Hebrew words that denote what rises or escapes (like vapor). The basic image is that of something visible yet immaterial that ascends and disperses.
H7008.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to denote either the smoke of a literal fire (Genesis 19:28) or metaphorically a vapor or fog (Psalms 119:83 and 148:8). In Genesis 19:28, it is the visible and terrifying sign of the destruction of Sodom. In the Psalms, the word takes on a broader significance: it represents either the suffering of the righteous (119:83) or a manifestation of divine power and order in creation (148:8). The meaning fluctuates between the concrete (physical smoke) and the figurative (fog, darkness, distress).
H7008.portee: The smoke rising from Sodom reminds us that God's judgment is real and visible — it is not an abstraction, but a power that manifests in the created world. For the psalmist, feeling "like a wineskin in smoke" expresses deep suffering, but also trust: even in the trial that obscures and dries up, God remains the one who governs all things. Thus, smoke becomes a sign of both divine justice and human fragility.

sens: one who opposes, who fights against someone
one who resists or obstructs
declared enemy or rival
H7009.detail:
1. The adversary is one who takes a stand against someone else, who actively opposes. They are an antagonist, a rival in a conflict. In Job 22:20, Job's adversaries are those who fight against him or resist him.
2. The word can also refer to one who simply obstructs or hinders, without necessarily seeking destruction. This is the opponent or the contradicter.
3. By extension, it refers to the enemy in a broader sense — one with whom one is not in agreement and against whom one acts. The context of Job evokes personal enemies whose downfall one rejoices in.
H7009.origine: The Hebrew word קִים (qim) comes from a root meaning "to rise" or "to stand up." The adversary is thus one who stands against someone, who rises as an obstacle. This image of someone standing up to fight explains why the word denotes opposition and hostility.
H7009.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 22:20. Eliphaz addresses Job and tells him that his adversaries are annihilated and their wealth consumed by fire. In this context, Job's adversaries are presented as his personal enemies or opponents. The text suggests that one should rejoice in their destruction — an idea that Job himself will reject, as he does not see these people as his true enemies.
H7009.portee: This verse reminds us that true victory over our adversaries is not our vengeance or personal triumph. The context of Job invites reflection on who our true enemies are and how our faith should transform our relationship to conflict and hostility.

sens: official order from a king or supreme authority, publicly promulgated and having the force of law
decision endowed with sovereign authority and intended to be respected
H7010.detail: 1. A decree is a solemn command issued by a king or an authority recognized as sovereign. In Daniel 6:7, the officials of the Persian kingdom ask King Darius to issue a "royal decree" prohibiting any prayer to anyone other than him for thirty days: it is an official order pronounced with the solemnity of royal power. 2. This decree, once confirmed by the king, acquires an irrevocable and absolute character. In Daniel 6:15, the text specifies that "the law of the Medes and Persians requires that any prohibition or decree confirmed by the king be irrevocable": in other words, once signed, the decree cannot be abrogated, even by the one who issued it.
H7010.origine: The Hebrew word קְיָם (qeyam) is related to a root meaning "to stand" or "to exist." The decree is something that "stands" firm and durable, which has weight and stability. It is an order that "stands up" like an inevitable and permanent law, hence the idea of something established, immutable.
H7010.emploi: The word appears twice in the book of Daniel, in chapters 6:7 and 6:15, both in the context of the Persian court of King Darius. In these two passages, it denotes royal ordinances endowed with the supreme authority of the sovereign. The first occurrence emphasizes the solemn nature of the royal proclamation ("royal decree"), while the second stresses its irrevocable and inviolable character once confirmed by the king according to the law of the Medes and Persians. This usage reflects the absolute authority of ancient Near Eastern monarchs.
H7010.portee: This word reminds the believer of the gravity of the commitment made before God and the importance of the word given. When a Persian king confirmed his decree, he could not revoke it: similarly, God's promises are irrevocable and stand firm forever. The account of Daniel 6 also shows how a servant of God can refuse to obey an unjust decree and prefer to face judgment rather than deny his faith.

sens: To remain standing, to be stable and solid
To persist, to continue to exist over time
To recognize or acknowledge as established and durable
H7011.detail:
1. The word first evokes solidity: something that holds firm, that does not collapse. In Daniel 6:26, the living God "stands" eternally — He is there, stable, unshakeable, like a foundation that nothing can shake.
2. It then signifies continuity over time: the ability to persist, to remain in force. The kingdom of God "stands" — it does not disappear, it endures from generation to generation.
3. In Daniel 4:26, the word takes on a particular nuance: "to recognize" what stands, is to acknowledge that something established, valid, remains true — it is to recognize a solid and permanent reality that imposes itself.
H7011.origine: The Hebrew קִיַּם (qiyyam) comes from a root that expresses standing, stability. The related word קוּם (qum, "to rise," "to stand up") reveals the basic image: what stands is what holds up, that does not collapse. The meaning evolves from physical posture (to remain standing) to perseverance (to remain in place over time), then to the recognition of an established reality.
H7011.emploi: The word appears twice in the book of Daniel, in the two major royal declarations that frame his story. In Daniel 4:26, Nebuchadnezzar is invited to recognize (or let stand as established) the fact that the God of heaven governs. In Daniel 6:26, the same king publicly acknowledges that the God of Daniel stands eternally — His existence is unshakeable, His dominion endures. These two usages show a God whose power remains stable in the face of changing human kingdoms.
H7011.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize a solid truth: God stands, meaning He remains, He will not fail. In a world of instability and change, this certainty of His permanence and eternal stability is a foundation of trust and hope. It is also a call to acknowledge and recognize this reality in one's own life.

sens: Action of standing up or getting up
Moment when someone rises or begins to move
H7012.detail:
1. The word designates the concrete action of moving from a sitting or lying position to a standing position. In Lamentations 3:63, the prophet says, "Look when they are sitting and when they rise": he speaks of those precise moments when his mockers change their posture, sitting then standing.

2. By extension, it evokes the moment when someone takes action, rises to act. It is the moment of transition from inactivity to movement.
H7012.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of standing up or rising. This root is related to the image of a person or object lifting up from the ground or a low position.
H7012.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided biblical text, in Lamentations 3:63. It is found in a passage where the prophet Jeremiah describes the contempt he is subjected to: he observes his enemies "when they are sitting and when they rise," in other words, he is mocked by them constantly, in all their gestures and at all their moments.
H7012.portee: This verse reminds us that contempt and mockery can accompany the believer at every moment of their life. Like Jeremiah, we may experience constant hostility, but this description in Lamentations also shows us how to face despair honestly and call upon God as a witness to our suffering.

sens: Weapon of war: long pointed stick or blade, wielded by a soldier on foot or horseback
H7013.detail: 1. The spear is an offensive weapon composed of a long shaft and a sharp point, which the warrior brandishes or throws against the enemy. It is a heavy and formidable weapon: that of Ishbi-Benob weighed three hundred shekels of bronze, making it extremely deadly and difficult to handle (2 Samuel 21:16).
H7013.origine: The Hebrew word קַיִן (qayin) comes from the root קוק (quq) which designates anything that is pointed or sharp. It is a concrete, simple term that names the object as it exists: a very ancient hand or projectile weapon, present among all the peoples of the Near East.
H7013.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 21:16, in the account of the battle between David and the giants of the race of Rapha. The usage emphasizes the impressive aspect of the enemy: this giant spear, forged from solid bronze, symbolizes the power and threat that weighed upon Israel. This context is that of David's last wars against the Philistines and their allies.
H7013.portee: This passage reminds us that David, despite his advanced age, had to face formidable enemies; but like in his youth, God was with him. The mention of this terrible weapon shows that Israel's victory was not due to the strength of arms, but to God's faithfulness.

sens: Member of the Kenite tribe, a nomadic people of the Sinai desert
Inhabitant or descendant of the city of Cain in Palestine
H7014A.detail:
1. The Kenites are a tribe of nomads who lived in the desert regions between southern Palestine and the mountains of Sinai. They are known as blacksmiths and metal workers. Moses' father-in-law, Jethro, belonged to this people, which shows the peaceful contacts between Israel and the Kenites in the early days (Numbers 24:22 speaks of their future fate).
2. Cain is also the name of a small town in Judea, listed among the cities of the territory of Judah (Joshua 15:57), which may refer to its inhabitants or a place of passage.
H7014A.origine: The name "Kenite" comes from the Hebrew *Qeynî*, related to the root *qayin* which means "blacksmith" or "one who works with metal." The people derive their identity from their trade: they are the artisans of fire and metal in the desert. The tribe bears the name of its function, which was common in ancient Near Eastern societies.
H7014A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Segond. In Numbers 24:22, in the prophecy of Balaam, the fate of the Kenites is mentioned in relation to Assyria — an indication that this people will be affected by future invasions, although they were allies of Israel. In Joshua 15:57, "Cain" refers to a city in the territory of Judah, listed alongside Gibeah and Timnah. These two usages show that the name applies both to a nomadic people and to a territorial establishment.
H7014A.portee: The Kenites remind readers that the people of God have never developed in isolation: God allowed other peoples and cultures to live alongside Israel, including in kinship ties (Jethro the Kenite becomes a wise counselor for Moses). This illustrates Israel's openness to just neighbors, even before the Law of Sinai.

sens: The firstborn son of Adam and Eve
The first murderer, who killed his brother Abel
A man under God's judgment and curse
A name that has become a symbol of fratricidal crime and rebellion against God
H7014B.detail:
1. Cain is the firstborn son of Adam and Eve, presented at the beginning of humanity after creation (Genesis 4:1: "she conceived and bore Cain"). His name means "possession," evoking an acquired good or plunder, perhaps reflecting the hope that a child represents.
2. Cain becomes the first murderer in history by killing his brother Abel, driven by jealousy: while the Lord accepted Abel's offering, He rejected Cain's, which provoked anger and fratricidal murder (Genesis 4:3-8).
3. After this crime, Cain receives an irrevocable judgment from God: he is cursed, wandering and a fugitive on the earth (Genesis 4:11-16), but God places a protective mark on him so that he will not be killed in vengeance.
4. The story of Cain illustrates how sin, born in the human heart even before the law, leads to rebellion, jealousy, and crime. His name remains attached to the first mortal transgression.
H7014B.origine: The Hebrew name Cain (קַיִן) literally means "possession" or "acquisition," suggesting the idea of possessing or creating. According to Genesis 4:1, Eve says in giving birth: "I have formed a man with the help of the Lord," showing that the name expresses the action of obtaining or producing. It is an ancient Hebrew name, given to the first generation of humans born of human parents.
H7014B.emploi: Cain appears thirteen times in the Bible, concentrated almost entirely in chapter 4 of Genesis where the foundational drama unfolds. He is first mentioned at his birth (Genesis 4:1), then during his offering to the Lord (Genesis 4:3). The narrative focuses on the internal conflict: first rejected by God, Cain is filled with bitter anger (Genesis 4:6), then he succumbs to sin by killing Abel (Genesis 4:8). After his crime, Cain is condemned to wander far from the presence of God (Genesis 4:16), marked with a divine sign. His story concludes with his descendants, notably Enoch and Lamech. The name becomes a biblical archetype of the murderer and the rebel.
H7014B.portee: The story of Cain reveals that sin arises from the human heart even in the absence of written law, and that jealousy, the mother of violence, can possess the soul to the point of murder. It also shows that God's judgment is just but tempered with mercy: even the guilty will not be destroyed. For the Christian, Cain serves as a warning against envy and rebellion against God, and an invitation to examine one's own motives and emotions, lest sin take root and lead to destructive acts.

sens: Nomadic people from Arabia related to Moses by marriage
Social group of itinerant blacksmiths and craftsmen
Descendants of Hobab, Moses' father-in-law
H7014G.detail:
1. The Kenites are a nomadic people from the Arabian desert, known for their ties to Moses: Hobab, their leader, was Moses' father-in-law (Judges 4:11). They lived in tents and moved from place to place.
2. This people were renowned for their skills in forging and metalwork: they were called itinerant craftsmen. They traveled with their tools, offering their services wherever they went.
3. In the account of Judges 4:11, Heber the Kenite had separated from the rest of his people and set up his camp near Kadesh, showing that they were never fully sedentary but adapted their way of life according to circumstances.
H7014G.origine: The name Kenites comes from a root meaning "blacksmith" or "metal worker" in Hebrew. This etymology reflects their main occupation: forging and making tools. Their reputation as expert blacksmiths is linked to their nomadic lifestyle, which allowed them to move between tribes and villages to offer their artisan services. The connection to Moses through his marriage to Zipporah, daughter of Hobab the Kenite, integrates this people into the history of Israel from its origins.
H7014G.emploi: The Kenites are mentioned only once in the Segond with this exact term (Judges 4:11). They appear as a distinct people, recognized by the Israelites for their expertise and independence. Although they are not prominent in biblical narratives, they play a symbolic role: they represent a foreign group coexisting peacefully with Israel, united by family ties and economic exchange. Their presence illustrates the reality of neighboring peoples and marital alliances of that time.
H7014G.portee: The Kenites remind us that the people of Israel were never isolated but were part of a network of peoples, families, and trade exchanges. Their familial link with Moses emphasizes that God works through human alliances, even with strangers. Their expertise and reputation also invite respect for well-done work and craftsmanship, which God values in His creation.

sens: Song of mourning sung at the death of an important person
Lamentation expressing pain and regret
Prophetic word announcing impending disaster or ruin
H7015.detail: 1. The funeral lament is a solemn song that is pronounced when someone great dies — a king, a prince, a city. David composed one for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:17): it is a public act that honors the deceased and expresses the grief of the people. 2. It is a lamentation, a complaint filled with emotion: it is cried out, sung with pain. The women of Israel learn to teach each other laments (Jeremiah 9:20), as a form of mourning art. 3. In the mouths of the prophets, the lament becomes a prophetic warning — the announcement of disaster that will befall a city or a people. Ezekiel pronounces a lament over Tyre to announce its destruction (Ezekiel 26:17): the funeral song becomes a word of divine judgment.
H7015.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to lament," "to weep." The lament was a common literary genre in the ancient Near East: it was sung to honor the dead and publicly express mourning. It is both a ritual and poetic act.
H7015.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophets Ezekiel (9 occurrences), Jeremiah (4 occurrences), and Amos. In David's time, it was composed for great figures (2 Samuel 1:17; 2 Chronicles 35:25). In the prophets, it changes meaning: it is no longer a song of mourning for the dead, but a dramatic warning addressed to the living about their future punishment. Ezekiel pronounces laments over Tyre (26:17), over Egypt (32:2), announcing their ruin. Amos does so as well (5:1). The prophetic context gives the word a force of announcing judgment.
H7015.portee: The lament shows that mourning and regret have their place in biblical faith — we do not hide pain, we sing it. It also teaches that there is a moment when words must take the form of a solemn complaint, in the face of death or God's judgment. For the Christian, it reminds us that to weep is human, and that God hears even our groans.

sens: City of Judah at the southern border of the territory
H7016.detail: Kina is a small city mentioned in the list of localities in southern Judah, near the border with Edom. It appears in the enumeration of cities belonging to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:22), alongside Dimona and Adada.
H7016.origine: The Hebrew name קִינָה (qinah) literally means "lamentation" or "complaint"; but when it designates this city, it is a proper name that does not carry this figurative meaning. Archaeologists have proposed various identifications for this site in the Negev, the desert region of southern Judah.
H7016.emploi: Kina appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:22, in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the territory after the conquest. It is among the localities of the southern Negev, indicating the extent of Judah's territory to the south up to the border with Edom.

sens: nomadic people of the Sinai desert and southern Palestine
tribe of blacksmith artisans
clan from which Moses' father-in-law came
H7017.detail:
1. The Kenites are a nomadic people established in the deserts between southern Palestine and the mountains of Sinai. They live in tents (Judges 5:24) and roam the arid regions of the south. Balaam describes them as having "a solid dwelling" and a "nest set on the rock" (Numbers 24:21), a poetic image of their life as nomadic shepherds in rocky high places.
2. The name literally means "blacksmiths" or "metal workers": it was a tribe of artisans specialized in forging and making metal tools, a trade passed down from father to son (1 Chronicles 2:55).
3. Hobab, Moses' father according to the biblical text, and his descendants belong to this people. Some members, like Heber and his wife Jael, settled near Kadesh in Canaan and formed an alliance with the inhabitants (Judges 4:11, 4:17). Jael became famous for killing Sisera, the enemy leader of Israel, in agreement with her own people (Judges 5:24).
H7017.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "forge" or "blacksmith" — the striking of metal on the anvil. This was their characteristic occupation and their tribal name. The Kenites formed a community of professional metallurgists, a group of clans linked by their craft rather than by a single genealogy.
H7017.emploi: The Kenites appear ten times in the Bible, mainly in historical narratives. They are first mentioned as an established people during Abraham's time (Genesis 15:19), then become famous through their connection with Moses — his father-in-law was a Kenite (Judges 1:16, 4:11). During the judges, Heber the Kenite lived peacefully with Canaan (Judges 4:11, 4:17), while his wife Jael took a decisive action in favor of Israel (Judges 5:24). Later, in the time of David and Saul, the Kenites remained respected allies: Saul spared their lives during his campaign against the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:6), recognizing the good they had done to Israel (1 Samuel 30:29).
H7017.portee: The Kenites remind us that God established bonds of friendship and alliance between Israel and other peoples: Moses' father-in-law was a stranger who wisely counseled him (Exodus 18). This people shows that divine protection for Israel extended to those who stood alongside His people. It is also a model of peoples who live according to their own vocation — metallurgists and nomads — while maintaining peace with the people of God.

sens: pre-flood man, son of Enosh and father of Mahalalel
patriarch of great longevity living before the flood
H7018.detail:
1. Kenan is one of the patriarchs of primitive humanity, son of Enosh and father of Mahalalel. He occupies a place in the genealogy of the early men: Genesis 5:9-14 reports his birth when his father Enosh was ninety years old, followed by his extraordinarily long life.

2. Like all men before the flood, Kenan lived an impressive number of years: nine hundred and ten years in total (Genesis 5:14). He fathered Mahalalel at seventy years and continued to live more than eight hundred years more, which testifies to the exceptional longevity characteristic of that time. His name also appears in the genealogy of Luke (Luke 3:37, where he is called Cainan in Greek).
H7018.origine: The Hebrew name Kenan means "possession." It belongs to the lineage of Seth and appears in the "official" genealogy of humanity, transmitted by Israelite tradition. This same character is named Cainan (in Greek Καϊνάν) in the New Testament.
H7018.emploi: Kenan is mentioned six times in the French Old Testament, all occurrences found in chapter 5 of Genesis or in 1 Chronicles 1:2. This passage from Genesis 5 enumerates the ten patriarchs before the flood with a regular formula: name of the father, age at the birth of the son, total lifespan, and mention of other children. Kenan fits into this solemn enumeration, no more and no less. The numerical data provided (seven hundred years after the birth of Mahalalel, nine hundred and ten years of total life) are part of the context of the flood and the renewal of humanity through Noah.
H7018.portee: Kenan reminds the reader that the genealogy of Christ is rooted in very ancient humanity, long before Abraham. His presence in the biblical genealogies—especially in Luke 3:37 where Jesus is presented as a descendant of this distant ancestor—underscores the continuity of the divine promise through the ages and the importance that God attaches to human history from its origins.

sens: The summer season, after spring and before autumn
Ripe fruits and harvests that come to maturity during summer
By extension, the wealth and agricultural abundance of a region
H7019.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the warm season of the year, when the sun shines the brightest. It is the natural period of rest in the cycle of time: "Summer and winter, day and night shall not cease" (Genesis 8:22), meaning that these regular rhythms will continue forever.

2. More concretely, the word speaks of the fruits that summer produces—figs, raisins, pomegranates—which are harvested in this season and eaten fresh or preserved. David sends his men "two hundred loaves, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits" (2 Samuel 16:1), which is nourishing and sweet food that has been stored.

3. The word can also mean the harvest itself, everything that grows in summer. When Jeremiah says, "they made an abundant harvest of wine and summer fruits" (Jeremiah 40:12), he speaks of the entire vintage and summer gathering. It is a sign of a fertile land and divine blessing.
H7019.origine: The Hebrew word קַיִץ comes from a root that denotes the heat and burning of the sun—hence the idea of summer, the scorching season. It is related to other words that express dryness and withering. In Aramaic, the neighboring form קַיִט also means "summer." The word paints the image of a season marked by solar intensity.
H7019.emploi: The word appears about twenty times in the Bible, mainly in the books of poetry and prophecy. It designates either the season itself (Genesis 8:22, Psalms 74:17) or the fruits it produces. Proverbs uses it to praise the one who gathers his reserves in summer (Proverbs 10:5: "he who gathers in summer is a wise son"), or to criticize the one who sleeps during this crucial season. The prophets use it to describe the abundance of a prosperous region or, conversely, the loss of that abundance in times of war: Amos's vision of a basket of summer fruits symbolizes the imminent end of Israel (Amos 8:1-2). The word can finally evoke absence: "The harvest has passed, summer has ended, and we are not saved" (Jeremiah 8:20).
H7019.portee: This word reminds the reader that God regulates the seasons and that they return regularly—a sign of His faithfulness. Summer and its harvests also symbolize a time of grace and opportunity: it is the moment to gather, to work, to be vigilant. Missing the summer season is to let the blessing pass by. It is a subtle yet powerful image of spiritual urgency: today is the time to receive what God offers.

sens: which is at the end, at the end of a series
which concludes, which finishes something
located beyond, at the limit
H7020.detail:
1. The word describes what is at the end of a row or succession: the "finishing" curtain in Exodus 26:4 is the one that closes the series, completing it to the end. It is the idea of the last link in a chain, the one that cannot go further.
2. By extension, it qualifies what marks the end of a set: in the four passages of Exodus concerning the Tabernacle, the "finishing curtain" is referred to as the one that concludes each assembly of curtains, where the final blue cords must be fixed (Exodus 26:10). It is what completes, stabilizes, and finalizes the structure.
3. The word can also evoke what is beyond, at the extreme limit: not the center, but the ultimate periphery, the edge.
H7020.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to cut," "to sever," or "to finish." This initial image of cutting, of what cuts and ends, has developed into a figurative sense: what is "cut" or marked is what comes last, what delineates the limit. This family is found in other terms describing the end, the conclusion, or separation.
H7020.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the detailed descriptions of the Tabernacle in Exodus 26 and 36. In these two parallel passages, it always qualifies the curtain that closes a series of assembled curtains: it is at its edge that the blue cords are fixed that bind the two sets of curtains together. The context is strictly architectural and cultic—the construction of the portable sanctuary. The meaning remains constant: the extremity, the last element of a succession that closes and completes the whole.
H7020.portee: This word reminds us that in God's work, every detail has its place and importance, down to the smallest elements that finalize and consolidate the whole. The "last" curtain is no less essential than the first: it is at its edge that the cords are tied that hold the entire structure of the Tabernacle. For the believer, this speaks of the importance of faithfulness to the end and the role of each person, even the humblest, in the completeness of God's project.

sens: A fast-growing plant that provides shade
A fragile plant, destroyed as quickly as it was born
What provides temporary relief
What can become a subject of superficial attachment
H7021.detail:
1. The castor oil plant is a fast-growing plant that God miraculously makes grow in one night to shade Jonah, who was suffering from the scorching desert sun (Jonah 4:6). It provides real physical relief: the plant rises above his head and protects him from the heat.
2. But this castor oil plant is also an extremely fragile plant: the next day, a worm pierces it, and it completely dries up in one night (Jonah 4:7). What came so quickly disappears just as quickly.
3. Jonah had become attached to this castor oil plant and felt great joy in its presence (Jonah 4:6), to the point that he despaired when it disappeared and cried out that it was a just cause to be angry — an excessive feeling for a mere plant (Jonah 4:9).
4. God uses this plant to teach Jonah a lesson: to have pity on a plant that one did not make grow and that is born and perishes in one night is to be mistaken about what truly deserves our compassion (Jonah 4:10). The castor oil plant becomes the image of misplaced concern.
H7021.origine: The Hebrew word קִיקָיוֹן (qiqayôn) likely refers to a castor oil plant or a shrub similar to it with broad leaves: perhaps the castor oil plant (Ricinus communis) from which oil was extracted, or a large gourd. The word is specific to the story of Jonah and rare in the Bible: it is only encountered in this account from chapter 4 of Jonah. The exact word evokes a plant that grows tall and spreads quickly.
H7021.emploi: The castor oil plant appears only four times in the Bible, all in Jonah 4:6-10. The text recounts how God makes it grow to protect Jonah from the sun, how it dries up immediately the next day, and how this event becomes the living parable of God's teaching to His prophet. The castor oil plant transitions from a providential plant to a symbol of foolish attachment to earthly and perishable things.
H7021.portee: This plant teaches the reader an important truth: we often become attached to temporary blessings and neglect what has true value, including compassion for lost souls. The castor oil plant also reveals our ingratitude toward God — we enjoy what He gives us without recognizing it for what it is, a fragile gift. Finally, it shows how God, with patience and tenderness, uses even a simple plant to teach us profound spiritual truths.

sens: Deep and lasting shame or dishonor
Serious harm to reputation or honor
Humiliating and public disgrace
H7022.detail:
1. Ignominy is a deep and lasting shame, one that marks and stains forever. In Habakkuk 2:16, the prophet announces to the tyrant that his drunkenness and nakedness — symbols of his humiliation — stain his glory; it is ignominy that will cover him, like a permanent stain.
2. It is also a serious dishonor that affects a person's reputation and honor. The prophetic context shows that this ignominy is not a mere passing affront, but a ruin of the guilty person's honor: where he aimed for glory, he will find only shame.
H7022.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of lightness, insignificance, or contempt. Ignominy is what makes someone despicable and light in the eyes of others, stripping them of dignity. It is the absolute opposite of glory and honor.
H7022.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Habakkuk 2:16. The prophet uses it to express divine judgment on the tyrant and the violent: while he was intoxicated with conquest and power, God will cover him with ignominy. This prophetic context shows that ignominy is the fate reserved for those who despise God and oppress the weak.
H7022.portee: This word reminds the reader that all pride and abuse of power lead to shame, and that God brings down the proud. Ignominy is not merely a passing punishment, but the definitive downfall of one who opposes God. For the believer, it is an assurance that divine justice will be fulfilled.

sens: Vertical surface of stone or brick enclosing a building or space
Interior surface of a room or structure
Obstacle or barrier that surrounds or protects a city
Wall of an altar or religious structure
H7023.detail:
1. The wall is the solid vertical surface that forms the outer walls of a house or building. It is what is seen when looking from the outside or inside. In 1 Kings 6:27, the wings of the cherubim in the temple touch the walls on either side, showing how the wall delineates the interior space.
2. Inside a structure, the wall is the partition that separates rooms or spaces. When Saul throws his spear in 1 Samuel 19:10, the wall receives the blow instead of David, showing that the wall protects the one who approaches it.
3. Around a city, the walls or ramparts are the massive fortifications that defend the inhabitants. In Ezekiel 23:14, Ezekiel sees paintings on the walls of a city, showing that the walls are visible and decorated.
4. Finally, the wall can refer to the side or surface of a religious structure such as the altar or temple. In Exodus 30:3, the sides of the altar are covered with gold, showing that the wall is a fundamental surface of the edifice.
H7023.origine: The Hebrew word קִיר (qir) comes from a root meaning 'to surround' or 'to enclose'. It belongs to the family of words designating constructions and enclosed spaces. The word evokes the image of a surface that encloses and protects: a wall exists only to delineate an interior from an exterior. In Hebrew, this word is very ancient and very common in all architectural descriptions.
H7023.emploi: The word appears 65 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in descriptions of buildings (the temple in 1 Kings 6, the structures in 1 Chronicles 29:4) and in Ezekiel's visions where he precisely describes the walls of the future temple. It can refer to the outer wall of a house (2 Kings 4:10), the interior wall of a room (Leviticus 14:37), or the walls of a city (Ezekiel 23:14). In rituals (Exodus 30:3, Leviticus 1:15), the wall or side of the altar is the point of reference. The word is also used figuratively: in Isaiah 25:4, God is a wall that protects the weak. Its meaning remains stable: always a solid, vertical surface that delineates or protects.
H7023.portee: The wall reminds the believer that God establishes limits and protections. It is an image of security: God builds walls for His people. But it is also an image of judgment: the walls of evil can collapse (Ezekiel 13:14). Meditating on the wall invites reflection on what truly protects us and what unjustly confines us.

sens: fortified city of Moab
H7024A.detail: Kir-Moab is a city of Moab (a neighboring kingdom of Israel, east of the Dead Sea), whose name literally means 'the wall of Moab' or 'the fortress of Moab'. The word קִיר (qir) means 'wall' or 'rampart' in Hebrew, and here designates a fortified city. In the only passage where it appears (Isaiah 15:1), the prophet Isaiah announces its destruction as part of God's judgment on Moab: 'The night it is ravaged, Kir-Moab is destroyed!'
H7024A.origine: The name Kir-Moab combines two elements: קִיר (qir), which means 'wall' or 'rampart' in Hebrew, and Moab, the name of the kingdom. The word קִיר evokes the image of a city surrounded by walls, thus fortified and defended. This city was an important administrative or military center of Moab.
H7024A.emploi: Kir-Moab appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 15:1, in the context of a prophecy against Moab. The prophet announces its total destruction in one night, illustrating the power of divine judgment against the enemy nations of Israel. It is likely the ancient capital or a major city of Moab, mentioned here to symbolize the complete annihilation of the Moabite kingdom.

sens: Ancient region of origin for the Arameans, likely in Mesopotamia
Place of exile where the Assyrians deported the inhabitants of Damascus
H7024B.detail:
1. Kir is an ancient region, probably in Mesopotamia, from which the Arameans (the inhabitants of Syria) originally came. This is where the Syrian people originated, as noted by Amos (Amos 9:7).
2. Kir became famous in the history of Israel as the place where the king of Assyria sent the inhabitants of Damascus, the capital of Syria, into exile after his conquest (2 Kings 16:9). The prophets Isaiah and Amos announce that this same fate of exile awaits them again (Isaiah 22:6; Amos 1:5).
H7024B.origine: The name Kir literally means "wall" in Hebrew. The exact location of this region remains uncertain to this day, but it is generally situated in Mesopotamia, likely to the southwest, near the Tigris or Euphrates. It is the historical home of the Aramean people before their dispersion.
H7024B.emploi: Kir appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in connection with Syria and the Arameans. The Bible first mentions Kir as the homeland of the Syrians (Amos 9:7), then as the place of exile where Assyria deported the inhabitants of Damascus in 732 B.C. (2 Kings 16:9). The prophets Isaiah and Amos later refer to it as a threat: divine judgment will lead the Syrians to experience the same exile, the same return to Kir (Isaiah 22:6; Amos 1:5). It is a symbol of exile and judgment for Damascus.
H7024B.portee: Kir reminds the people of God that divine judgment extends to all nations, not just Israel. For the believing reader, it is a lesson in humility: human powers, even an empire like Assyria, are merely instruments of God's will. Exile is never the final word in God's plan.

sens: Fortified city of the kingdom of Moab, major capital or stronghold
Fortress symbolizing Moabite power and wealth
H7025.detail: Kir-Haréseth is one of the two main fortified cities of the kingdom of Moab, rivaling Moab the capital. Its name literally means "wall of pottery" or "wall of shards," perhaps because its walls were built or decorated with fragments of ceramics, or simply because it stood on a mound strewn with ancient debris. During the military campaign against Moab reported in 2 Kings 3:25, Kir-Haréseth remains the last stronghold; it is where the king of Moab entrenches himself with his best troops when all the other cities fall. In the eyes of the prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah, this city represents the threatened greatness of the Moabite kingdom — its accumulated wealth, power, and political prestige. When Kir-Haréseth falls or is besieged, it is the entire Moab that falters.
H7025.origine: The Hebrew name קִיר חֶרֶשׂ consists of "qir" ("wall," "fortification") and "chéreseth" ("pottery" or "ceramic objects"). It is not an ordinary word, but a local Moabite proper name, probably given to the city for its characteristic constructions or its particular archaeological site.
H7025.emploi: Kir-Haréseth appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always referring to this city of Moab. It occupies a central place in the account of 2 Kings 3, where it is the last Moabite bastion against the coalition of Israel, Judah, and Edom. The other three occurrences are found in prophetic oracles — in Isaiah 16 and Jeremiah 48 — both of which announce the misfortune of Moab. The prophets mention it in lamentation, as it symbolizes the pride of the Moabites and their impending destruction: its inhabitants mourn over its ruins, its people groan over their lost possessions. The name does not change much from source to source, although the Segond offers three variants: Kir-Haréseth, Kir-Hérès, and Kir-Harès, which reflect slightly different pronunciations of the same place.

sens: Head of a family among the temple servants who returned from exile
H7026.detail: Kéros is a man mentioned twice in the Bible during the return from exile to Jerusalem. His name means "peg" or "joint" in Hebrew, but it is primarily his role that matters: he is the head of a family of temple servants, the "sons of Kéros," who are part of the group that returns from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple (Ezra 2:44; Nehemiah 7:47). These temple servants formed a lower class of cultic personnel, distinct from the priests and Levites.
H7026.origine: The name Kéros comes from the Hebrew qéros, which literally means "peg" or "joint of the foot." Although it is a Semitic name, its etymology evokes a part of the body, which was common in Hebrew onomastics. The biblical context shows that Kéros is a name borne by a real man from the time of the return from exile.
H7026.emploi: Kéros is mentioned only twice in the Scriptures, in chapters 2 and 7 of the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, in nearly identical lists. These two passages enumerate the families of temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel under the reign of Cyrus the Persian. The repetition of his name in these two parallel lists emphasizes the administrative and cultic importance of his family in the restoration of Jewish religious life after the Babylonian exile. Kéros represents a part of the people who, although enslaved or servants, participated in the return and reconstruction of the temple.

sens: Father of King Saul, of the tribe of Benjamin
H7027G.detail: Kis is a Benjamite, a man of worth and good family, who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He is best known as the father of King Saul: when Saul begins to prophesy with the prophets, people are astonished and say, "What has happened to the son of Kis?" (1 Samuel 10:11), showing that the name of the father was well known and that the fulfillment of Saul's royal role was unexpected. Kis belongs to the family of Matri, in the tribe of Benjamin, and himself descends from a long genealogy (1 Samuel 9:1).
H7027G.origine: The name Kis means "bent" or "folded," perhaps evoking a posture of humility or submission. It is a Hebrew name borne by several men in the history of Israel: besides the father of Saul, the Bible mentions an ancestor of Mordecai and other Levites named Kis, which shows that it was a common name among the tribes of Israel.
H7027G.emploi: Kis appears about a dozen times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the early books of Samuel and in Chronicles. Most of the time, he is mentioned as "father of Saul" (1 Samuel 9:1, 10:11, 14:51), which was his main distinction in national history. He is described as "a mighty and valiant man" (1 Samuel 9:1), suggesting that he was respected and influential in his community. The genealogies in Chronicles list him among the descendants of Benjamin, confirming his importance in the tribal structure of ancient Israel.
H7027G.portee: Kis embodies the lineage and heritage through which God chose to place Saul as the first king of Israel. Although Kis himself is not a main character in the Bible, the respect accorded to his name reminds us that God often works through families and generations to accomplish His purposes. The story of Saul, beginning with Kis's search for his donkeys (1 Samuel 9), shows how God directs ordinary human events toward His extraordinary ends.

sens: A Levite from the family of the Merarites
son of Mahli and grandson of Merari
H7027H.detail: Kis is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi dedicated to the service of the Temple. He specifically belongs to the family of the Merarites, descendants of Merari, one of Levi's three sons. He is the son of Mahli (1 Chronicles 23:21) and the brother of Libni and Eleazar. His name means "bent" in Hebrew, an image of a bend or inclination. Kis had at least one son, Jerahmeel, whose descendants are listed in the genealogies of the Temple (1 Chronicles 24:29).
H7027H.origine: The name Kis (קִישׁ) literally means "bent" or "folded," perhaps evoking a posture of humility or submission. He is not to be confused with King Saul of Benjamin, who also had a father named Kis: these are two distinct individuals from different genealogies. The name appears in the genealogical records of the Levites, particularly those of the Merarites, compiled during the reorganization of the Temple under King David.
H7027H.emploi: Kis appears three times in the Book of Chronicles, exclusively in the genealogical lists of the Levites responsible for the service of the Temple. All occurrences are found in chapters 23-24 of Chronicles, which enumerate the organization of the Levitical families. He is mentioned as the son of Mahli (1 Chronicles 23:21), his sons are recognized as heirs after the childless death of his brother Eleazar (1 Chronicles 23:22), and his descendants are listed again in 1 Chronicles 24:29. These references show that Kis held a respectable place in the Levitical genealogy, with recognized descendants.

sens: A Levite from the family of the Merarites, son of Abdi, during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah
H7027I.detail: Kis is a Levite from the tribe of Levi, belonging to the branch of the Merarites. He is the son of Abdi and lived during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah, likely in the 8th century BC. He appears in the account where the Levites rise up to purify the temple after a period of religious neglect (2 Chronicles 29:12).
H7027I.origine: The name Kis means "bent" or "leaning" in Hebrew. It is a common name in the Old Testament, borne by several individuals, including the father of King Saul and an ancestor of Mordecai. In this case, it designates a descendant of Merari, who himself was one of Levi's three sons, the founder of the priestly tribe of Israel.
H7027I.emploi: Kis appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 29:12. He is mentioned as one of the Levites who participate in the restoration of worship in the temple during the time of King Hezekiah. His name is included in a list of Levites responsible for this important work of religious reform and cleansing of the defiled sanctuary.

sens: Ancestor of Mordecai mentioned in the Book of Esther
H7027J.detail: Kis is a Jewish man from the tribe of Benjamin, living during the time of the Exile and the Return. He appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 2:5, as the grandfather of Shimei and the father of Mordecai's father. Mordecai, who will be the hero of the Book of Esther alongside Queen Esther, is a direct descendant of this Kis: it is through this genealogical line that Mordecai's Benjamite and Jewish origin is learned.
H7027J.origine: The name Kis (קִישׁ) means "bent" or "folded" in Hebrew, evoking a bent posture. It was borne by several important men in Israel's history, including the father of King Saul. The Kis mentioned in Esther 2:5 belongs to a different genealogical branch but bears the same name.
H7027J.emploi: Kis appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 2:5, where he is cited as an ancestor of Mordecai. Mordecai is presented as "the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kis, a man of Benjamin." This genealogy emphasizes Mordecai's Jewish and Benjamite identity, which is important for understanding the context of the Book of Esther, where a Jew raises a queen in the palace of the king of Persia. The name Kis holds only genealogical and contextual significance here.

sens: Stream of central Palestine
Site of divine judgment against Israel's enemies
H7028.detail:
1. The Kison is a watercourse that flows through central Palestine. Its name literally means "winding stream," which aptly describes its character: a river that flows in meanders. It is a small river, not a large permanent watercourse, but during the winter rains it can become fierce and devastating (Judges 5:21: "The torrent of Kison swept them away").
2. The Kison is first the site of the miraculous victory of Deborah and Barak against Sisera, commander of King Jabin's army (Judges 4:7 and 4:13). This stream becomes the place where God breaks the military power of the enemy: Sisera's nine hundred iron chariots are defeated there, likely swept away by a providential flood. This is why the psalmist recalls this memory as an example of God's judgment (Psalms 83:10).
3. The Kison is also the place where the prophet Elijah executes the four hundred fifty prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:40), marking the definitive triumph of the true God over idolatry. Each time the Bible mentions the Kison, it is thus in a context of divine judgment and deliverance for Israel.
H7028.origine: The name "Kison" comes from the Hebrew verb meaning "to bend" or "to wind," which evokes the tortuous appearance of a stream winding through the valley of Jezreel in Galilee. It is a natural stream in the region, but the Bible names it especially because it becomes the backdrop for two spectacular interventions of God: the defeat of Sisera and the execution of the false prophets.
H7028.emploi: The Kison appears five times in the Bible, always in major contexts. Three times in the account of Deborah (Judges 4:7, 4:13, Judges 5:21), where this stream becomes the unwitting instrument of God's judgment: either by engulfing Sisera's army or by symbolizing the divine power that crushes the enemies. Once in the account of Elijah on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:40), where the prophet leads the priests of Baal to the Kison to put them to death, thus marking the triumph of the true God over idolatrous worship. Finally, the psalmist alludes to it as a distant but memorable example of God's judgment (Psalms 83:10). In each occurrence, it is a place of victory and judgment.
H7028.portee: The Kison reminds the reader that God judges the enemies of His people and that He even uses nature—a simple stream—as an instrument of His will. It is also a call to trust: when Deborah and Barak trust God despite the apparent military superiority of the enemy, God intervenes. Finally, the judgment on the prophets of Baal at the Kison shows that God does not tolerate idolatry and fiercely defends His honor and the purity of worship. These two events, long after, continue to encourage believers to rely on God's justice and power.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Merari, father of the musician Ethan
H7029.detail: Kishi is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe dedicated to the service of the temple. He belongs to the branch of Merari and lived during the time of King David. He is best known as the father of Ethan, a renowned musician or minstrel who served in the temple (1 Chronicles 6:44). Kishi is one of those anonymous figures in the Old Testament whose legacy is primarily that they fathered notable men of God.
H7029.origine: The name Kishi literally means "bow of the Lord" or "bow of the Eternal"—an image of strength and protection that suits a Levite of priestly lineage. The text of 1 Chronicles 15:17 also mentions him under the name Kushaiah, a variant of the same character.
H7029.emploi: Kishi is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:44. He appears in the genealogy of the Levitical singers and musicians of the temple during David's time. His importance comes less from his own actions than from his place in the genealogical chain: son of Abdi and father of Ethan. The latter is listed among the renowned musicians established by David for the worship of the Ark of the Covenant.
H7029.portee: Kishi reminds us that the musical and liturgical excellence of the temple had deep familial roots: talents were passed down from generation to generation, and even obscure names in the sacred text carried the blessing of serving the Eternal. His existence illustrates the invisible importance of those who, without being kings or prophets, form the foundation of authentic worship.

sens: String musical instrument
Orchestral instrument in Babylonian worship
Symbol of pagan royal power
H7030.detail:
1. A guitar is a stringed musical instrument that is plucked or strummed to produce sound. It is among the instruments that made up the Babylonian royal orchestra, alongside the trumpet, the pipe, and other varied instruments (Daniel 3:5).
2. In the account of Daniel 3, the guitar plays a religious role: it accompanies the sound signal that commands the entire population to bow down before the golden statue erected by Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:7). The sound of this instrument was heard by all peoples, nations, and men of every language.
3. This instrument symbolizes the power and splendor of the Babylonian king: its melodies were intended to seduce and submit the peoples to the worship of the false deity represented by the statue.
H7030.origine: The Hebrew word קַתָרֹס (qataros) is borrowed from a foreign Semitic language, probably ancient Greek or Aramaic. In the Hebrew and Aramaic Bible, this word appears only in the Aramaic text of the book of Daniel, reflecting the cosmopolitan context of Babylon. It designates one of the instruments imported or used by the Persian and Babylonian royal court.
H7030.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Bible, all occurrences found in chapter 3 of the book of Daniel (verses 5, 7, 10, and 15). These verses recount the same event: King Nebuchadnezzar's order to worship the golden statue he erected. The guitar is mentioned as one of the six or seven instruments of the royal orchestra that signaled everyone to bow down. The context remains the same — the orchestration of a religious ceremony of false worship — and the word fits within the vocabulary of musical instruments used to manipulate crowds through sensual seduction.
H7030.portee: The account of Daniel 3 reminds the Christian reader that artistic beauty and pleasant sensations can serve to seduce towards idolatries. Even in the face of a grand spectacle orchestrated by the power of the world, believers must remain vigilant and not let their emotions divert them from their faithfulness to the true God. The story of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shows that refusing this magnificent spectacle in the name of obedience to God liberates and saves.

sens: Moving with speed and lightness
Quick, acting fast
Figuratively: insignificant, of little weight or importance
H7031.detail:
1. The word primarily describes physical speed and lightness of movement. Asahel had "feet as light as a gazelle of the fields" (2 Samuel 2:18), an image that shows someone capable of running fast and without heaviness. It is the quality of one who runs, jumps, or moves with apparent ease.
2. It also characterizes one who acts with promptness and swiftness. The "swift messengers" of Isaiah 18:2 are envoys who cover distances quickly. Similarly, in Joel 3:4, the verb "very quickly" conveys this ability to do something without delay.
3. By extension, the word can evoke what is light in the sense of being insignificant or trivial. In Ecclesiastes 9:11, "the race is not to the swift" means that even the fastest, the most suited, does not control the outcome: everything depends on time and circumstances, not just speed.
H7031.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of lightness and speed. It is linked to the image of movement without weight, of what does not become heavy. It appears in other Hebrew words describing liveliness, agility, or even (in some contexts) moral or spiritual insignificance.
H7031.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, primarily to describe beings or messengers whose speed is remarkable. In 2 Samuel 2:18, it depicts Asahel as an extraordinarily fast runner. In Isaiah, it qualifies the messengers sent to the nations (18:2) or the pursuers in a flight (30:16). In Jeremiah 46:6 and Lamentations 4:19, it emphasizes the impossibility of escaping during military pursuits: even the fastest cannot flee. The context is often warlike or of divine judgment, where human speed proves futile against the will of God.
H7031.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that human strength, speed, or skill are not enough to ensure salvation or victory. Ecclesiastes 9:11 is the key lesson: everything depends on time and circumstances, that is, on the hand of God. Even the most capable man, if he refuses divine wisdom, remains vulnerable.

sens: Sound produced by the speech or cry of a person
Noise or sound produced by a musical instrument
Word, what is said
Reason, motive, cause of an action
H7032G.detail:
1. The sound of the human voice, that which is heard when someone speaks or cries. In Daniel 6:20, the king calls Daniel "with a sad voice": one can hear his emotion in the tone and intensity of his voice.
2. The noise or sound of a musical instrument. Daniel 3:5 lists several instruments — the trumpet, the guitar, the sambuca — whose "sound" is heard: it is the musical noise they produce.
3. What is expressed by the word, the statement itself, what is said. When speaking of "arrogant words" in Daniel 7:11, it refers to what has been said, the content of the word.
4. The cause, the motive, what justifies an action or judgment. In Daniel 7:11, "because of the arrogant words" means that it is for this reason, because they were spoken, that the beast is killed.
H7032G.origine: This Aramaic word (the language of Daniel 6-7 and some passages of Ezra) corresponds exactly to the Hebrew word קוֹל (qol) which appears hundreds of times in the Hebrew Old Testament. At the time of the New Testament, Greek uses φωνή (phonè) to translate these two words. The root primarily designates what is heard, the sound that comes from a source and strikes the ear. From there, it extends to the meaning of word, then of reason or cause.
H7032G.emploi: This Aramaic word appears 6 times in the book of Daniel, in chapters 3, 6, and 7. The first three uses (Daniel 3:5, 3:7, 3:10) speak of the "sound" of musical instruments that are heard at the moment of bowing down. The fourth (Daniel 3:15) repeats the same expression. In Daniel 6:20, it is the "voice" of King Darius calling Daniel from the lion's den, with the emotion suggested by the adjective "sad." In Daniel 7:11, the word means rather "cause" or "motive": it is because of the arrogant words of the horn that the beast is judged and destroyed. The apocalyptic context gives this last use a legal significance: the reason for divine judgment.
H7032G.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that God hears and understands what is said: the voice of cries of oppression, the voice of arrogance and rebellion. God's judgment is never blind — He sees and He listens. Even a voice pleading from the depths of the pit, like Daniel's, does not go unheard.

sens: Sound produced by the speech or cry of a creature
Expression of someone's thought or will
H7032H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the sound emitted by a person who speaks or cries — what comes out of the mouth and spreads through the air. In Daniel 4:31, it is literally a voice that descends from heaven to deliver a message to King Nebuchadnezzar at the moment he speaks a word: the physical moment when the sound is heard.
2. But this voice is never empty: it always carries content, an intention. That is why it can also mean the message itself, the communication of a thought or will. Here again in Daniel 4:31, it is a voice that speaks, commands, and conveys the divine decree — it is thus the very expression of the power and intention of the one who speaks.
H7032H.origine: In Aramaic, qal (קָל) is the exact counterpart of the Hebrew word qôl (קוֹל, H6963), which literally means "sound" or "noise." These two words likely come from a root that evokes the idea of something that manifests, resonates, and becomes perceptible. In both Hebrew and Aramaic, the voice is always linked to a living and conscious presence, never just a simple noise.
H7032H.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:31, in a vision of King Nebuchadnezzar. The context is solemn: the king boasts of his power and his constructions in his own palace, and it is at that very moment that a voice from heaven resounds. This voice is not a mere sound disturbance: it carries a divine judgment, announcing that the king will be stripped of his kingdom. The use of the word in Aramaic, rather than in Hebrew, emphasizes that the narrative is presented as the word of the pagan king himself, transcribed in his own language.
H7032H.portee: In this passage, the divine voice that resounds from heaven reminds the Christian reader that God speaks — and that His word imposes itself on the greatest kings of this world. It is a call not to confuse human prestige or earthly power with the reality of God's judgment. The voice from heaven is the active and audible presence of the One who truly judges and governs.

sens: Cook or dry by the heat of fire
Be consumed or burned
Devour, consume (figurative sense: a burning pain)
H7033.detail:
1. To roast means to cook or dry something over fire. In Leviticus 2:14, roasted grain is presented to the Lord as a firstfruits offering: it is wheat cooked over fire, then ground. In Joshua 5:11, the Israelites eat roasted grain after Passover — a cooked and prepared food.
2. To be burned or consumed by fire, often completely. Jeremiah 29:22 reports that the king of Babylon roasted Zedekiah and Achab in the fire: the image is one of complete destruction by fire.
3. To consume or devour in a figurative sense, like an intense pain. In Psalms 38:8, the psalmist says that a burning evil devours his insides — this is not a real fire, but a suffering that consumes from within as a fire would.
H7033.origine: The Hebrew verb קָלָה (qalah) comes from a root expressing the action of heating or burning. It literally describes the effect of fire on a material: the change in color, texture, and composition caused by heat. The word is used for cooking grain (a practical, hardened, and preservable food) and extends to the sense of destruction by fire. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb may correspond to Greek words related to the action of burning or consuming.
H7033.emploi: The verb קָלָה appears 4 times in the Old Testament, always with a sense of cooking or destruction by fire. Two uses concern the ritual or daily preparation of food: the roasted grain offered to the Lord (Leviticus 2:14) and that eaten by the Israelites (Joshua 5:11). One use is figurative: the psalmist's suffering consumed like an inner fire (Psalms 38:8). The last is a threat of violent destruction: the king of Babylon roasts the princes (Jeremiah 29:22). The meaning thus shifts from the concrete (cooking food) to the image of suffering and judgment.
H7033.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the cooking or roasting of grain, a daily and nourishing act, was at the heart of Israel's worship: even simple food was offered to God. The image of fire that consumes, in a figurative sense, expresses the reality of inner suffering and divine judgment. For the believer, this vocabulary invites us to see that God takes our inner pains seriously and judges injustices with certainty.

sens: Lose one's dignity, honor, be lowered before others
Be regarded as worthless, insignificant, or of little importance
Be treated with contempt or disdain
Suffer public shame or humiliation
H7034.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the act of losing one's honor or dignity — it is to be abased, lowered. When someone strikes another beyond the set limit, his brother must fear that he will be "despised in your eyes" (Deuteronomy 25:3): the bruised body becomes the visible sign of a loss of dignity.
2. It also means to be regarded as worthless, counted for nothing. David describes himself as "a poor man of little importance" (1 Samuel 18:23) — not despicable in himself, but socially insignificant, without weight. Similarly, it is "better to be of a humble condition" (Proverbs 12:9) than to pretend to glory without having enough to eat: true shame is not poverty, but lying.
3. The word can express active contempt, unjust treatment: to despise one's father and mother is a crime that calls for a curse (Deuteronomy 27:16). "The worthless man" oppresses the honored one (Isaiah 3:5) — not because he has no value, but because he is rejected, devoid of status.
4. Finally, it evokes humiliation: the glory of Moab, once so great, will soon be reduced "to an object of contempt" (Isaiah 16:14), becoming as short and vain as the contract of a mercenary who works for the allotted time and then leaves.
H7034.origine: The Hebrew verb קָלָה (qalah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of lightness, of little weight.
