3. To create, form (in the sense that God creates a people): Eve says, "I have formed a man with the help of the Lord" (Genesis 4:1). It is God who has created and possesses his people (Psalms 74:2: "remember your people whom you have bought").
4. To possess as a master or owner: the word expresses the idea of holding something as one's own, like wealth or an inheritance received and held.
5. To acquire knowledge or wisdom through study or experience: Proverbs 16:16 contrasts "acquiring wisdom" with gold, showing that knowledge is conquered as a precious possession. Proverbs 4:5 invites to "acquire wisdom."
H7069.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "creating" or "producing," hence "to create a possession" and by extension "to buy." The verb carries the image of constituting something new, of appropriating it. The root also evokes creation in the sense that God "creates" (that is, forms) a people by redeeming them. The word is found in Aramaic as קְנָא (qena), which carries the same commercial and possessive meaning.
H7069.emploi: The verb appears 75 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the narratives of Genesis, Exodus, and Leviticus. It primarily denotes the purchase of land (Genesis 25:10, 33:19, Joshua 24:32), then of slaves (Exodus 21:2, Leviticus 25:44-50). In the spiritual domain, it describes the creation of the people by God (Exodus 15:16, Psalms 74:2) and the acquisition of wisdom and knowledge (Proverbs 4:5, 4:7, 16:16). In Ecclesiastes, it denotes the accumulation of goods (Ecclesiastes 2:7). The wisdom texts use it to exhort to "acquire" wisdom and understanding rather than riches.
H7069.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God does not merely command: he creates a people and possesses them as his most precious acquisition. It is a personal and costly act on God's part. On the other hand, the biblical call to "acquire wisdom" (Proverbs) invites the reader to make the knowledge of God and justice as precious a possession as gold, which must be conquered and preserved like a treasure.

sens: Stem or ramification that comes from a plant
Stem or reed used as a measure or instrument
Bar or rigid stem serving as support or structural piece
H7070G.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a stem or branch that grows from a plant, particularly the reed or aquatic stems. This is the basic image: a stem that extends from a main stem. In Exodus 25:32, six branches come out from the sides of the lampstand, like the branches that extend from the trunk of a tree.

2. By extension, this word applies to reeds or stems used as measuring and calculating tools. A reed served as a standard unit of measure — about six cubits — for measuring buildings and distances, like a ruler or a modern meter. Similarly, a branch of the lampstand is not a real plant, but a metal stem deliberately shaped to resemble a plant structure.

3. The word also designates rigid bars that form the structure of objects: the bar that supports the trays of a balance (the beam), or the stems of the golden lampstand that form the worship in the Tabernacle. In Exodus 25:36, "the branches of the lampstand" form a forged whole from a single piece of pure gold.
H7070G.origine: The Hebrew word קָנֶה (qaneh) comes from a root that evokes the idea of a straight and hollow stem. Reeds and bulrushes, very common in Egypt and the Promised Land, are its starting image. Words from the same family also designate sugarcane and narrow, elongated elements. This word concretely translates the observation of nature: a stem that divides or extends, capable of serving both as a plant and as a tool.
H7070G.emploi: This word appears about 22 times in biblical Hebrew, almost exclusively in instructions related to the Tabernacle, particularly in the description of the golden lampstand (candelabrum) in Exodus 25 and 37. Each occurrence describes the six branches that extend from the four sides of the central lampstand: three on the right, three on the left. The lampstand is not a vegetal object, but a piece of goldsmithing; the term "branches" is chosen because the structure resembles a tree or plant, a symbol of life. The instructions emphasize that the branches, the bowls (decorative elements), and the central stem form "one piece," highlighting the unity of divine design. This word never applies to real tree branches in the provided passages: its use remains strictly cultic and architectural.
H7070G.portee: The six-branched lampstand, described with this word, is a major symbol in the faith of Israel and in the New Testament: it represents the luminous presence of God among His people. Each branch burning pure oil (as in Exodus 27:20) evokes the light of God that spreads in all directions, without fragmenting. This image of unity in multiplicity — a single piece of gold, six distinct branches — invites the Christian reader to meditate on how God manifests in creation and in the Church, as a unique light that shines in various paths. This is why the lampstand becomes a symbol of the Holy Spirit and the Word of God in both Jewish and Christian traditions.

sens: aquatic plant with a straight and hollow stem, growing in marshy areas
long and rigid object used to measure distances
structural piece of an object (stem of a plant, beam of a balance, arm of a lampstand)
fragile or weak thing, easily broken
littoral or wetland area where reeds grow
aromatic or fragrant spice
H7070H.detail:
1. The reed is primarily a true aquatic plant with a hollow and straight stem, growing in marshes and wet areas (Psalms 68:31 speaks of "the beast of the reeds," referring to the hippopotamuses that live in these places). Isaiah 42:3 celebrates how Christ will not break "the bruised reed" — the image evokes a fragile, wounded stem that could be destroyed but is spared tenderly.
2. By extension, the reed becomes an object of measurement: it was used as a measuring rod to assess distances. Ezekiel receives a messenger who "had in his hand a measuring reed" (Ezekiel 40:3), a precision instrument to explore the future temple.
3. The word also designates the stems or structural pieces of certain objects: the stem of the golden lampstand (Exodus 37:17), the arm or the "stem" by which this sacred utensil stands.
4. It is used for the rods or measuring bars that balance scales: these are the "reeds" that allow for fair weighing.
5. Metaphorically, the reed evokes weakness and instability: Egypt is like a reed that the king of Assyria can break (Isaiah 36:6).
6. The word can also refer to calamus, an aromatic plant imported, from which a precious spice or perfume is derived, mentioned in the ingredients of the sanctuary (Exodus 30:23 and Isaiah 43:24).
H7070H.origine: The Hebrew word קָנֶה comes from a root that evokes the idea of a straight and hollow stem. This root is linked to the concept of elevation and verticality. In Arabic, words from the same family also designate the cane or the reed. The basic image is that of a plant that stands upright, rigid but fragile, characteristic of the reed in the wetlands of the Levant. This plant was well known in Egypt and Mesopotamia; it served as a common material (for mats, roofs, instruments).
H7070H.emploi: The word appears 26 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah). Its primary meaning of aquatic plant is rare (Psalms 68:31); much more often, it designates an instrument or part of an object: in the Tabernacle and the Temple (lampstand, scales, measures), and in the prophetic visions of Ezekiel who describes the future temple using a "reed" to measure (Ezekiel 40 passim). Isaiah uses it metaphorically to evoke the fragility of Egypt in the face of the Assyrians. The context of Exodus 30:23 and other passages also shows its use as a precious spice or perfume (calamus).
H7070H.portee: The reed, in prophetic preaching and in the Gospel, symbolizes human fragility: it is what bends and breaks easily. Jesus makes it the image of the wounded heart that He does not destroy, but heals with compassion (Isaiah 42:3). The measuring reed or cane also reminds us that God measures and judges with justice and precision: His plans are reliable and His promises exact.

sens: An aquatic plant with a hollow and elongated stem
A rigid and graduated measuring instrument
A unit of length based on this measure
H7070I.detail:
1. The cane is primarily a plant of wet areas, with a hollow and flexible stem — the reed or aromatic calamus. This natural stem served as raw material to make useful objects.
2. By extension, this word designates a rigid stick used to measure distances and dimensions. It is a common working instrument among carpenters and architects. Ezekiel is commanded to measure the temple with a cane (Ezekiel 40:6).
3. The cane also becomes a standard unit of length — generally six cubits. When Ezekiel measures the sides of the future temple in "canes," he translates its dimensions: five hundred canes to the east, north, south, and west (Ezekiel 42:16-19).
H7070I.origine: The Hebrew word קָנֶה (qaneh) primarily designates the aquatic plant we call reed. Its concrete image — a long, straight, and hollow stem — naturally makes it a measuring tool. The same word is used for stems, branches, long bones of the body, and even the branches of the temple lampstand. This root also appears in Akkadian and Aramaic with similar meanings.
H7070I.emploi: This word is used five times in the Bible, exclusively in Ezekiel to measure the future temple. The angel guiding Ezekiel hands him a cane to take the precise dimensions of the restored sanctuary: the width of the threshold, then the four sides of the temple enclosure. It is a tool of architecture and prophetic vision. The context is always one of exact measurement and orderly construction.
H7070I.portee: The measuring cane symbolizes divine precision: the restored temple is not vague or approximate, but conceived in its smallest details by God Himself. For the reader, this affirms that God's plan for His people and His worship is perfectly defined and trustworthy. It is an invitation to see the rigor and order in the divine design.

sens: The joint that connects the arm to the shoulder
The place where the arm bone fits into the shoulder
H7070J.detail:
1. The joint that connects the arm to the shoulder — this is the point of junction between the arm and the body. Job 31:22 speaks of this joint as something that could "detach," which shows how this word denotes a physical link, a fragile fitting. If this joint were to break, the arm would be paralyzed.
2. By extension, the Hebrew word קָנֶה originally designated the hollow stem (like that of a reed or cane); the meaning "joint" derives from this: just as a reed articulates in segments, the shoulder is the point where two segments of the body articulate with each other.
H7070J.origine: The word קָנֶה is fundamentally based on the idea of "stem" or "reed," which are plants formed of segments. This image of hollow segments articulated together led to naming the joint of the bones: a joint functions somewhat like the nodes of a reed, allowing flexibility and movement. The word thus migrated from the botanical world to the anatomical world.
H7070J.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible with the meaning of "shoulder joint." It is used in the context of a curse: Job, proclaiming his innocence, wishes that his shoulder detach if he has ever committed the injustice he is accused of. It is a powerful image of punishment — the loss of the use of the arm, which was a sign of curse in antiquity.
H7070J.portee: This word reminds us of the fragility of the human body. When Job invokes this curse on his shoulder, he acknowledges that our physical strength is nothing in the face of God's justice. For the believer, it is an invitation not to place trust in the strength of the arm or the ability to do evil with impunity, but to seek justice and honesty.

sens: Instrument used for weighing, with two pans suspended from a beam
Beam or bar that supports the pans of a scale
Image of divine judgment and equity
H7070K.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the complete instrument for weighing: the scale with its two pans where one places what one wants to compare. In Isaiah 46:6, the idolaters "weigh silver on the scales" to know its value and pay it to the silversmith.
2. More specifically, the word can refer to the horizontal beam (the "yoke") that supports the two pans and allows for balance — it is the main beam of the instrument.
3. By extension, the scale becomes the biblical image of judgment: weighing actions means evaluating them; a just scale speaks of equity. This symbolism helps to understand God's role in judging with precision.
H7070K.origine: The Hebrew word קָנֶה comes from a root that first evokes the stem, cane, or reed — flexible and hollow plants found near water. The same word is used to describe the stem of a lampstand (Exodus speaks of the golden lampstand with its branches and stems). The image of the stem has naturally extended to anything that is a stem or elongated beam, including the yoke of the scale, which resembles a horizontal bar. The context determines whether it is a reed, a measure, a part of the lampstand, or the weighing instrument.
H7070K.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond to designate the scale itself (Isaiah 46:6). Elsewhere in the Old Testament, the same Hebrew word takes on other meanings: it can mean the reed (aquatic plant), a measure of length (the reed of 6 cubits), or the parts of the golden lampstand of the Tabernacle. The context of Isaiah 46 is commercial and idolatrous: the pagans weigh silver practically to bargain for a metal god. It is a moment in the vision where the prophet critiques the absurdity of idolatry.
H7070K.portee: The scale invites the reader to meditate on God's just judgment. Unlike human injustice, God weighs all things with precision — our actions, our hearts, our intentions. For the believer, this reminds us that nothing escapes the divine gaze, and that we should not rely on riches or idols, but turn to the one who judges with equity.

sens: aquatic plant with a straight, hollow stem, or its stem
fragrant substance derived from a variety of reed, used in perfumery and rituals
H7070L.detail:
1. The reed is an aquatic plant that grows in wet areas and has a hollow, straight, and rigid stem. It is a familiar image in the Promised Land, where reeds line the waterways. The same Hebrew root also designates the measuring cane or the rigid stems of the sanctuary's lampstand.
2. By extension, the word designates calamus (or fragrant cane), a scented variety of eastern reed from which a precious and costly perfume was derived. In Song of Solomon 4:14, it is listed among the most precious aromatics, alongside spikenard, saffron, and myrrh. It is a luxury product, imported from afar, symbolizing beauty and wealth.
H7070L.origine: The Hebrew word קָנֶה (qaneh) comes from a root that evokes the idea of a straight and rigid stem. Due to the solid structure of the reed, the same word applies to other stem-shaped objects: the measuring cane, the branches of the golden lampstand of the Temple, and even the framework of the human body. The Greek word κάλαμος (kalamos), which often translates this Hebrew term, refers to both the reed and the writing pen.
H7070L.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, with two distinct meanings. In Song of Solomon 4:14, it refers to calamus, the fragrant reed, a precious trade product imported from distant lands. In Ezekiel 27:19, in the description of Tyre's trade, the fragrant reed appears again among the goods exchanged in the markets, highlighting its status as a luxurious and coveted item in antiquity.
H7070L.portee: The fragrant reed, a rare and aromatic object, speaks to our senses and reminds us that God cares about beauty and delicacy. In the Song, it evokes refined love and tenderness. Its precious nature and distant origin invite us to see how God's gifts circulate throughout the world and enrich our lives with a beauty that cannot be manufactured by ourselves.

sens: watercourse that marked a territorial boundary in the Promised Land
stream serving as a border between two tribes
H7071G.detail: 1. Kana is a watercourse, probably a stream or brook that flowed toward the Mediterranean in the Promised Land. The Hebrew word קָנָה means "reed," evoking the plants that grow along the water. 2. Geographically, this watercourse served as a natural boundary: in Joshua 16:8, it marks the southern limit of the territory of the tribe of Ephraim; in Joshua 17:9, it delineates the southern boundary of Manasseh to the north. These two passages show how God divided the lands among the tribes by natural landmarks, and the Kana stream was one of those landmarks that clearly separated the inheritances.
H7071G.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew root קנה (qanah), which means "reed." Reeds are characteristic plants of the banks of rivers and streams in the Middle East. The name of this watercourse thus reflects its nature: a stream where reeds grew, a natural feature that made it recognizable and ideal as a boundary between territories.
H7071G.emploi: Kana appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in the context of the division of the Promised Land. Joshua 16:8 makes it the western boundary of Ephraim, while Joshua 17:9 describes it as the southern border of Manasseh. In these two passages from the book of Joshua, Kana serves the same function: it is a concrete geographical marker that precisely defines where a tribe's inheritance begins or ends. The biblical text uses these topographical details to show that the division of the lands was neither arbitrary nor vague, but based on natural boundaries that everyone could recognize.

sens: City of the tribe of Asher marking its boundary
H7071H.detail: 1. Kana is a locality mentioned in biblical texts as a landmark delineating the territory of the tribe of Asher in the Promised Land. Its name means "reed" in Hebrew, likely evoking the vegetation of marshy areas or nearby waterways. It is listed in the Book of Joshua as one of the borders of Asher, alongside Ebron, Rehob, and Hammon.
H7071H.origine: The name Kana comes from the Hebrew קנה (qanah), which literally means "reed." This term refers to the aquatic plant that grows in wetland areas. The choice of this name for a city likely indicates that it was situated near a region rich in reeds, perhaps a watercourse or marshy land. This same root appears elsewhere in biblical Hebrew to designate the reed used as a measure or as a raw material.
H7071H.emploi: Kana appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Joshua 19:28, during the description of the boundaries assigned to the tribe of Asher after the conquest of Canaan. It is mentioned in a list of localities marking the limits of the tribal territory. This city was also known as Kana in Greek (Κανᾶ), which shows the continuity of the toponym through the centuries. Although little documented in the Old Testament, its existence is attested in the biblical geography of northern Canaan.

sens: Who cannot bear the sharing of a person's affection or loyalty
Who defends his right or honor with vigilant ardor
Attribute of God: He does not tolerate that His people prefer other gods
H7072.detail:
1. Jealousy is the feeling of one who fears losing or seeing shared what belongs to him — here, love, fidelity, honor. Joshua 24:19 speaks of the Lord as a jealous God: He demands exclusive loyalty and does not accept that His people serve other gods alongside Him.
2. Jealousy implies active vigilance: the jealous one watches to defend what is his and responds sharply to threats or offenses. Nahum 1:2 shows this vigilance turned into action: the Lord takes vengeance on those who are unfaithful to Him; He bears a grudge against His enemies.
3. Applied to God, this word expresses that the Lord demands an exclusive relationship with His people and does not share His glory with idols. It is a fundamental trait of His holiness: to require recognition as the only true God.
H7072.origine: The Hebrew word קַנּוֹא comes from the root קנא (qana), which fundamentally means "to be ardent," "to be inflamed." This root evokes an intense heat, like that of fire. The term applies to any passion that seizes the being — jealousy, envy, passionate zeal. In the Old Testament, this word often characterizes God's reaction when His honor or unique relationship with Israel is called into question.
H7072.emploi: This word appears twice in the Segond: in Joshua 24:19 and Nahum 1:2, always applied to God. Joshua uses it to warn Israel that serving the Lord cannot be done halfway: God demands unwavering fidelity and will not tolerate His people mixing their worship with that of the gods of neighboring nations. The prophet Nahum uses it to show that this divine jealousy is not passive: it manifests itself through vengeance against those who oppose God or are unfaithful to Him. In both cases, the word reveals the intensity of the bond that God claims with His people and His determination to preserve it.
H7072.portee: This word helps the Christian understand that God does not ask for a lukewarm or shared commitment: He desires a whole relationship. God's jealousy is not a weakness or a flaw, but the expression of His demanding love and holiness. It invites the believer to recognize that fidelity to God does not tolerate compromise with the false gods of this world.

sens: Son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau, one of the chiefs of Edomite tribes
Ancestor of the people of Edom, living in the time of the patriarchs
H7073G.detail: 1. Kenaz is a direct descendant of Esau: he is the son of Eliphaz (who is himself the son of Esau) and is among the twelve sons or grandsons of Esau who became chiefs of tribes. He is mentioned alongside his brothers Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gaetham, and Amalek (Genesis 36:11, 36:15). 2. As a chief of the Edomite tribe, Kenaz bears the title of "chief" or "duke" and appears in the genealogical lists of Edom that show how the nation of Esau organized into distinct peoples (Genesis 36:42; 1 Chronicles 1:53). He represents a branch of Esau's family established in the region of Edom, south of Canaan.
H7073G.origine: The name Kenaz means "hunter" in Hebrew, evoking a man skilled in hunting. He belongs to the genealogy of Esau and his descendants, the Edomites, who formed a brother nation to Israel but were often in conflict with it. The name regularly appears in the genealogical lists of Edom, indicating its importance in Israel's tradition.
H7073G.emploi: Kenaz is mentioned five times in the Bible, all in the genealogies of Esau: three times in chapter 36 of Genesis (verses 11, 15, and 42) and twice in 1 Chronicles 1 (verses 36 and 53). These usages are purely genealogical: they place Kenaz in the family tree of Edom and list the chiefs of Edomite tribes. No narrative or action is attributed to him. It simply serves to remind that Kenaz, as the son of Eliphaz and brother of other chiefs, was part of the ancestors of the Edomite people.

sens: Brother of Caleb, father of Othniel
H7073H.detail: Kénaz is a man of the Old Testament, brother of Caleb (son of Jephunneh) and father of the judge Othniel. He appears in the genealogy of the children of Caleb in 1 Chronicles 4:15, where he is named among the direct descendants of Caleb in the tribe of Judah.
H7073H.origine: The name Kénaz means "hunter" in Hebrew, evoking the image of a man skilled in hunting. It is a name borne by several characters in the time of the patriarchs: it is also found among the chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:42), descendants of Esau. In the lineage of Caleb, this name marks belonging to a family of warriors and judges.
H7073H.emploi: Kénaz is mentioned only once in the Bible that has come down to us, in 1 Chronicles 4:15, as the son of Caleb and father of Othniel. This mention situates him in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, a few generations after the entry into Canaan. His son Othniel became one of the great judges of Israel, suggesting that Kénaz was the father of a family of important military and spiritual leaders.
H7073H.portee: Kénaz reminds the reader that the great men of the Bible had fathers and lineages: Othniel, the first judge of Israel, was the son of Kénaz. This shows that God often works through families of faith, and that a pious lineage can bear fruit over several generations.

sens: Character from the time of the conquest of Canaan, father of Othniel the first judge of Israel
H7073I.detail: Kenaz is a man whose lineage is known: his son Othniel becomes the first judge of Israel, delivering the people from oppression (Judges 3:9-11). Kenaz is also the brother or close cousin of Caleb, one of the two faithful spies during the Exodus from Egypt. It is through this family connection that he is situated in the history of Israel: he belongs to the generation that conquers Canaan or whose children conquer it (Joshua 15:17).
H7073I.origine: The name means "hunter" in Hebrew. The form "Kenizzite" is also encountered (Numbers 32:12), which designates a family or clan. Two Kenaz appear in the Old Testament: one is a chief of Edom, son of Eliphaz (himself the son of Esau); the other, to whom the provided roles belong, is the father of Othniel and brother or relative of Caleb.
H7073I.emploi: Kenaz appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the context of the conquest of Canaan and the time of the judges. The first four occurrences mention his son Othniel who takes the city of Debir and receives Acsa in marriage (Joshua 15:17; Judges 1:13 and 3:9-11); the last lists his descendants in the genealogy of the Judeans (1 Chronicles 4:13). Kenaz himself does not receive direct action in the narrative; he is known through his son and his connection with Caleb.
H7073I.portee: Kenaz illustrates how the faith of the ancients is passed down from one generation to another: he, who belongs to the community of the Exodus from Egypt, sees his son Othniel become a deliverer of the people, empowered by the Spirit of God. It is a reminder that our children inherit faith and that God can use them to deliver His people.

sens: people or clan descended from Kenaz
H7074G.detail: The Kenizians are a people mentioned only once in the Bible, at the moment when God enumerates to Abraham the nations that inhabit the land He promises him. The name means "descendants of Kenaz," an ancestor about whom little is known. They appear in the list of peoples of the Levant alongside the Kenites and the Kadmonites (Genesis 15:19).
H7074G.origine: The name comes from Kenaz, who appears in the genealogies of Edom and Judah as an ancestor of warrior clans. The Kenizians are simply referred to as "descendants of Kenaz" ("kenizzi" = "kenizzi"). It is unclear whether Kenaz was a distinct historical figure or a tribal eponym invented to explain the origin of a group.
H7074G.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 15:19, in the discourse where God enumerates to Abraham the peoples occupying the Levant that his descendants will conquer. The Kenizians are listed alongside other small peoples of the ancient Levant: Kenites, Kadmonites, Hittites, Perizzites, and others. This enumeration aims to show the extent of the promise and the diversity of the inhabitants of the land.
H7074G.portee: This mention reminds us that Abraham receives a promise concerning a land inhabited by many peoples. It shows that possessing the land will require an action from God, since the territory is occupied. For the Christian reader, it is an opportunity to meditate on how God fulfills His promises beyond visible human obstacles.

sens: person belonging to the tribe or clan of Kenaz
member of a family established in the Near East
descendant of a lineage of warriors and leaders
H7074H.detail:
1. The Kenizian is a member of the family group descended from Kenaz, a man who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. The term designates his descendants, those who are "of the clan of Kenaz" — a genealogical and social identification, as one would say "a Judean" or "a Benjaminite".

2. Historically, Kenaz was an ancestor whose descendants had settled in the Near East. The mention of Caleb as a "Kenizian" (Joshua 14:6) shows that this group had its own recognizable identity at the time of the conquest of the land.

3. Spiritually, the term carries the mark of faithfulness to the Lord. Caleb is presented as the Kenizian who "fully followed the way of the Lord" (Numbers 32:12; Joshua 14:14), suggesting that belonging to this group came with a reputation for devotion to God.
H7074H.origine: The word comes from Kenaz (קְנַז), an ancestor who lived during the time of the stay in Egypt and the desert. Kenaz was the father of Othniel, the first judge of Israel (Judges 3:9-11), and of Seraiah, which confirms his genealogical importance. The suffix "-i" (קְנִזִּי) marks belonging to this clan, as in French one says "Parisian" for an inhabitant of Paris. The family of Kenaz integrated into the people of Israel and maintained a distinct identity recognized in biblical genealogies.
H7074H.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible, always to designate Caleb, son of Jephunneh. In Numbers 32:12, it is encountered during the judgment on the generation of the desert: only Caleb the Kenizian and Joshua are allowed to enter Canaan because they "fully followed the way of the Lord." In Joshua 14:6 and 14:14, Caleb presents himself to the people of Israel by his genealogy "Kenizian," reminding that his heritage from Hebron comes from his past faithfulness. The usage shows that the term affirms both a family belonging and a spiritual reputation of loyalty to God.
H7074H.portee: For the Christian, the Kenizian represents someone who, although of an origin outside the main tribe of Israel, is distinguished by his unwavering attachment to the will of God. The story of Caleb the Kenizian teaches that faithfulness to the Lord is not a matter of tribe or birth status, but of heart and obedience. It encourages the believer to remain attached to God even when all around him doubt.

sens: What one possesses, what one has bought or accumulated
Herd, livestock, material wealth
Creature, living being that one possesses
Property, land ownership
Goods, wealth in general
H7075.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to what one has acquired through purchase or labor — something that one did not originally possess but has appropriated. Esau "took all his livestock and all the goods he possessed, the herd that belonged to him, which he had acquired in the land of Canaan" (Genesis 36:6): these goods are the fruit of his settlement and efforts.
2. The word particularly designates the herd and livestock, the living wealth of the ancient patriarchs. In Genesis 34:23, the men of Shechem covet "their herds, their goods, and all their livestock" — livestock is here the primary form of wealth.
3. More broadly, it can refer to any creature or living being that one possesses, such as the slave "bought by the priest for money" (Leviticus 22:11) who counts among the "goods" of the priest.
4. The word can also refer to land and real property — "the Levites were not given a share in the land, except for cities to dwell in and the suburbs for their herds and for their goods" (Joshua 14:4): the goods here include the use of the land.
5. In a broader sense, it encompasses all accumulated material wealth. Psalm 104:24 celebrates "your goods" in speaking of all creation — everything that God has created and that fills the earth is His good, His possession.
H7075.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to acquire," "to procure," "to buy." It expresses the idea of taking possession of something, making it one's own. The family of the word also includes the verb "to acquire" and other nouns of possession. It is a concrete word: it always speaks of what can be actually possessed — a herd, land, a slave — never of an abstract or immaterial possession.
H7075.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the narratives of the patriarchs (Genesis) and in the laws (Leviticus). It almost always designates material wealth: the herds of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Genesis 31:18, 36:6), the goods coveted by the men of Shechem (Genesis 34:23), or the allocation of the Levites (Joshua 14:4). In the psalms and the prophets, it takes on a broader and more theological meaning: the "goods" of God that fill the earth (Psalm 104:24), the spoils and riches that enemies come to seek (Ezekiel 38:12-13). The meaning remains constant: what is possessed, what belongs to someone.
H7075.portee: This word reminds us that material wealth — herds, land, money — is always viewed as a possession: it belongs to the one who holds it, but it can also be lost, coveted, or reclaimed. For the Christian, this invites reflection on what truly belongs to us and on our responsibility toward what God entrusts to us. Every good that we accumulate is transient and can disappear; what matters is the wisdom to manage it well.

sens: Aromatic bark of a tropical plant, used as a spice and perfume
Precious and costly substance, imported from afar
Element of luxury and sensual seduction
Symbol of wealth and beauty in love
H7076.detail:
1. Cinnamon is the dried bark of a tropical tree, ground into powder or pieces: it emits a warm and sweet fragrance, highly valued. It is used to flavor, season, and preserve food. In Exodus 30:23, it is part of the composition of the holy anointing oil for the tabernacle, alongside myrrh and fragrant cane — precious materials that are difficult to procure.
2. It is a luxury commodity, imported from distant lands: its price is high, and only the wealthy or religious authorities can use it. The quantity required for the holy anointing oil (two hundred fifty shekels) shows its cost and prestige.
3. In the passages of Proverbs 7:17 and Song of Solomon 4:14, cinnamon adorns the body and the bed of the one who loves or is loved, enveloping love and seduction in the aroma of the most precious goods. It is an attribute of wealth and refined beauty.
H7076.origine: The Hebrew word קִנָּמוֹן likely comes from a neighboring Semitic language or is borrowed from a trade language with the Far East, from where this spice originated. The Greek cinnamômon and Latin cinnamomum have the same origin. The word literally designates the fragrant bark of the tree — raw material imported, symbol of the riches of the ancient world.
H7076.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 30:23, cinnamon is one of the noble aromatics that enter into the formulation of the anointing oil, reserved for divine worship and the tabernacle — a context of holiness and separation. In Proverbs 7:17 and Song of Solomon 4:14, it appears in lists of sumptuous perfumes that magnify romantic desire and the beauty of the beloved woman. In these three uses, cinnamon always embodies the rare, the precious, the delightful — never the everyday.
H7076.portee: Cinnamon reminds us that the Bible does not disdain sensory pleasures and material beauties: God Himself commands that the best perfumes be used for His worship (Exodus 30:23). Human love, in Proverbs and the Song, is adorned with these treasures without shame, as something good and beautiful. At the same time, the rare use of the word emphasizes that the precious and rare honor what they are reserved for: the Lord first, then true love.

sens: To build a nest, to settle in a nest
To make one's nest, to inhabit a high or protected place
To establish oneself somewhere, to take root
To find refuge or shelter
H7077.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to build and inhabit a nest. Birds nest in trees or rocks, like the stork in the cypress trees (Psalms 104:17) or the doves on the cliffs (Jeremiah 48:28).
2. The word also evokes the idea of settling somewhere durably and peacefully: it is finding a dwelling, a home. The serpent "makes its nest" (Isaiah 34:15) in a broader sense than simply building, it is creating its habitat.
3. By extension, "to nest" designates living or dwelling in a safe and high place: one who has their "nest" in the cedars of Lebanon (Jeremiah 22:23) imagines themselves protected and stable.
4. Ultimately, the word takes on a nuance of rooting: to establish oneself, to settle, to find a place to land and live.
H7077.origine: The Hebrew root קנן (qanan) literally means to create or make a nest. It is related to the idea of construction and creating a living space. The word can also evoke the idea of planting, rooting, like a bird that firmly establishes itself somewhere. The basic image is that of the nest: a careful construction, an intimate and protected refuge.
H7077.emploi: The verb appears five times in the Old Testament, always applied to creatures seeking shelter or habitat. It is used for birds (stork, vultures, doves, birds of the sky) that nest in trees or rocks, and even for the serpent (Isaiah 34:15). In Jeremiah 22:23, it is applied figuratively to the king of Judah who "has his nest in the cedars": it is an ironic allusion to his false security. In each occurrence, the word retains the idea of durable establishment in a protected or elevated place.
H7077.portee: This word reminds the reader that even voiceless creatures find refuge and homes according to God's plan. For the believer, it also evokes the necessity of finding in God one's true refuge, one's unshakeable spiritual "nest," unlike the illusory securities of earthly powers. The irony of Jeremiah 22:23 warns that no one can escape God's justice by clinging to seemingly impregnable positions.

sens: Net or trap set to capture an animal
Limit, end assigned to something
What stops or holds back the course of an action
H7078.detail:
1. The word first evokes a net or a trap: the image of what captivates and immobilizes. This is the concrete meaning of the Hebrew word.
2. It then comes to designate a limit or an end: what marks a stop, a conclusion. In Job 18:2, "when will you put an end to these speeches" literally means "when will you set a limit to your words," that is, when will you stop talking?
3. More broadly, it is what holds back or slows the normal course of something — a boundary, a threshold that one does not exceed.
H7078.origine: The Hebrew word קֵנֶץ comes from a root that evokes the idea of capturing or limiting. The primary meaning is that of a net or trap, which then metaphorically extended to any imposed limit or end. The family of this word in the Bible shares this image of restriction or capture.
H7078.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 18:2. Bildad addresses Job, asking him when he will put an end to his words: it is a reproach, as if he were saying that Job's words captivated him like a net. The context is that of a rhetorical contest where Job's friend reproaches him for speaking endlessly and without wisdom. The word captures well this tension between words flowing without limit and the need for a conclusion.
H7078.portee: This word reminds us that our words must have an end and wisdom. It invites us to recognize that unrestrained speech becomes a trap, both for the listener and for the speaker. Putting an end to what is vain is to show discernment.

sens: City of Gilead, in Transjordan, east of the Jordan
Possession or acquisition conquered by Nobach who renamed it
H7079.detail:
1. Kenath is a fortified city of Gilead, a mountainous region east of the Jordan. It appears in the conquest narratives when the tribes of Israel divide the lands (Numbers 32:42).
2. The name Kenath literally means "possession": it evokes a city taken and appropriated. This is exactly what happened: a man named Nobach conquered it and renamed it after himself as a sign of personal appropriation. Later, the city also changed hands, taken by the Geshurites and the Syrians (1 Chronicles 2:23).
H7079.origine: The name Kenath comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to possess," "to acquire." It is a name of possession, marking the right of ownership or control. By giving this name to the city, it emphasizes that it was conquered and appropriated—first by Nobach, then by other peoples later.
H7079.emploi: Kenath is mentioned twice in the Bible, in both occurrences of Numbers 32:42 and 1 Chronicles 2:23. The first time, it appears in the story of the land distribution after the conquest of the Jordan: Nobach, an Israelite military leader, seizes Kenath and the surrounding small towns, then names them after himself. The second mention, in the genealogies, recalls that it was with its satellite towns a possession of the descendants of Machir, father of Gilead—but that the Geshurites and the Syrians took it back. The name thus appears in two contexts: the initial conquest and the reminder of a subsequent loss.

sens: One who claims to know the future or hidden secrets by occult means
The practice itself of divination, prediction by magical arts
The words or oracles supposedly revealed by this practice
Figuratively: one who speaks in vain, without true knowledge
H7080.detail:
1. A diviner is a person who claims to have access to secrets or the future through magical or occult means—not through true prophecy inspired by God. Balaam was an example of this, and the Law absolutely prohibited this practice in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10). The Segond translates it simply as "diviner."

2. The word also designates the activity itself: practicing divination, that is, seeking to know the future through these forbidden means. When the Philistines called the diviners to find out how to return the ark of the Lord (1 Samuel 6:2), they were asking these men to "divine" the answer.

3. The words spoken by a diviner are called "oracles"—what he claims to have received or discovered. The text often refers to them as "vain divinations" or "lying oracles" (Ezekiel 13:9, Ezekiel 21:28), as they are empty of truth.

4. In a figurative sense, the word can qualify one who speaks without true knowledge, who claims a wisdom they do not possess. Isaiah 44:25 shows God proclaiming "foolish are the diviners": they speak with assurance, but it is empty.
H7080.origine: The Hebrew verb קָסַם comes from a root designating the action of dividing, sharing, cutting—as if one were dividing hidden signs to extract meaning. The word is linked to the idea of omens, signs that are interpreted. It is a very ancient practice, attested among the neighboring peoples of Israel and expressly condemned by the Mosaic Law, which opposes true prophecy from God to the false predictions of diviners.
H7080.emploi: The verb and its forms appear about twenty times in the Bible, especially in the books of the Law, the Prophets, and the Kings. Deuteronomy 18:10 places the diviner at the heart of the practices forbidden to Israel, alongside the magician and the astrologer. The Kings and the book of Samuel mention it in real history: the Philistines consulted the diviners (1 Samuel 6:2), and Saul sought a woman who practiced divination (1 Samuel 28:8). The Prophets, notably Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Micah, denounce the false prophets and diviners who deceive the people with "lying oracles" (Ezekiel 13:9) and "vain divinations" (Ezekiel 21:28). The word always carries an implicit condemnation: it is a lie disguised as wisdom.
H7080.portee: This word reminds the believer of a crucial distinction: between true prophecy, which comes from God alone and submits to His Word, and false predictions, which arise from human pride and the influence of evil powers. Prohibiting divination affirms that only God knows the future and that seeking elsewhere is a betrayal of faith. For today's Christian, it is a warning against any form of superstition or reliance on the false wisdom of the world.

sens: Practice of predicting the future by occult or magical means
Prophetic word or oracle from a diviner or magician
Enchantment, spell, or magical charm
Word of authority or wise decision (from a king or a judge)
H7081.detail:
1. The word qesem primarily refers to divination and magical practices through which one claims to know the future or influence events. This is the profession of diviners who, like Balaam in Numbers 22:7, are paid for their predictions, or of false prophets whom God condemns in 1 Samuel 15:23, where divination is equated with idolatry.
2. The qesem can also refer to the word itself spoken by the diviner or magician — the oracle, the prediction. Balaam in Numbers 23:23 "can do nothing against Jacob" because God does not allow his divinations to harm the people of God.
3. In the forbidden practices of Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10, 2 Kings 17:17), the qesem appears alongside enchantments and magic: it is a set of techniques intended to communicate with spirits or predict fate.
4. Proverbs 16:10 uses the word in a positive and entirely different sense: the "oracles" of the king are his wise and decisive words, which guide his judgment. Here, qesem means a word of authority inspired by wisdom.
H7081.origine: The word qesem comes from a Hebrew root that denotes the practice of divination and prediction. It may derive from a root meaning "to cut" or "to divide" (as one cuts spells or divides signs), or simply "to speak." The word describes both the act of divining and the result — what one claims to know through these occult means. The Old Testament regularly uses this word to condemn the divinatory practices of the nations, particularly of Canaan, which the Israelites were not to imitate.
H7081.emploi: The word qesem appears about 11 times in the Old Testament, mostly to condemn the magical and divinatory practices forbidden to Israel. It is first applied to Balaam, the diviner of the nations (Numbers 22-23), whose divinations God nullifies. It characterizes the false prophets and magicians in Jeremiah 14:14 and Ezekiel 13 and 21, who claim to know the word of God but lie. It is an abomination according to Deuteronomy 18:10 and a serious sin equated with idolatry in 1 Samuel 15:23. However, in Proverbs 16:10, the same word positively describes the words of the just king, which are like oracles of wisdom — showing that the word can qualify an authoritative and reliable word, not just a magical one.
H7081.portee: This word teaches Christians that seeking to know the future through occult means or to evade God's will through magic is a serious and barren temptation. Divinatory practices imply an autonomy from God that does not exist: God alone controls the future (Numbers 23:23). But the contrast with Proverbs 16:10 also invites the believer to listen to just and wise authoritative words as oracles of trust — to trust in God's guidance rather than the enchantments of the world.

sens: To forcibly remove, completely strip away
To take away, cut off (a part of a whole)
(Figuratively) To destroy, annihilate the essence of something
H7082.detail:
1. The word describes the action of tearing away or stripping something with force and completeness. In Ezekiel 17:9, the eagle "will tear away" the roots of the tree, meaning it will completely uproot it from the ground, depriving it of what nourishes it.
2. It also means to remove or cut off a specific part of a whole: the eagle will take away its fruit, separating it from the tree to which it was attached.
3. Figuratively, to tear away expresses destruction or annihilation: deprived of roots and fruit, the tree is doomed to wither, all its vital strength being torn away from it.
H7082.origine: The Hebrew verb קָסַס (qasas) expresses the fundamental idea of taking away, cutting off, or stripping. The starting image is physical: removing something by violently separating it from its support. This root belongs to the concrete vocabulary of deprivation and stripping.
H7082.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 17:9. It is used in a prophetic parable about two eagles and a tree: the first eagle will tear away the roots and the fruit of the tree planted by the river. The context is that of divine judgment on Jerusalem, depicted as a tree uprooted and stripped of everything that keeps it alive. The act of tearing away is presented as a process that requires neither great strength nor a large crowd.
H7082.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on the fragility of everything that is not rooted in God. Uprooting a plant from its roots removes it from its place of life and condemns it to death: it is a powerful image of divine judgment that strikes kingdoms and peoples who turn away from Him.

sens: small container or case worn at the waist to hold ink and writing instruments
symbol of scribal and administrative authority
H7083.detail:
1. An écritoire is a small container or case, typically worn at the waist, designed to hold ink and writing instruments. It is the professional equipment of the scribe. In Ezekiel's vision, the man dressed in linen "carrying an écritoire at his waist" (Ezekiel 9:2) has the necessary tools to mark the foreheads of the righteous who are to be spared during judgment.
2. The écritoire also represents scribal and administrative authority, the power to record, document, and decide. The one who carries it exercises a prominent official function. This is why it appears in a vision of divine judgment where only this celestial scribe can intervene to save the elect.
H7083.origine: The Hebrew word qeseth literally denotes a small container or case. It comes from a root evoking the idea of cutting or slicing, as scribes would cut their quills to write. This term is specific to the Hebrew Old Testament and reflects the importance of the scribal office in the administration and worship of Israel.
H7083.emploi: This word appears only three times in Ezekiel 9, all passages describing the same character: the man dressed in linen in the vision of the judgment of Jerusalem. The three uses employ the expression "carrying an écritoire at his waist" to identify this man as a scribe, an agent of divine judgment. His écritoire symbolizes both his administrative function and his salvific role: he will mark on the forehead those who are to be spared.
H7083.portee: This image of the écritoire reveals that God forgets none of His servants and that divine judgment is meticulously documented. It reminds the believer that, even in times of catastrophe, God keeps a record of His own and preserves them. The écritoire of the celestial scribe is the sign that our faithfulness matters to God and that we are written in His book.

sens: Fortified city of Judah
Place of refuge and conflict during David's flight
H7084.detail: Keilah was a fortress located in the lowlands of Judah, northwest of Hebron (Joshua 15:44). It primarily appears as the setting for a crucial episode in David's flight: harassed by Saul, David frees the inhabitants from Philistine raids and then takes refuge there with his companions (1 Samuel 23:2-4). Saul learns that David is there and besieges it, but the inhabitants, under pressure, threaten to deliver David to Saul (1 Samuel 23:11-12). David then flees with his men to the hills of the desert. Thus, Keilah becomes a symbol of the perils David faced and the ingratitude that even his acts of liberation could not guarantee.
H7084.origine: The name Keilah means "fortress" in Hebrew, evoking a stronghold intended for defense. It is a fortified urban center typical of the cities of Judah during the royal period. The name also appears in the lists of the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 3:17-18), where a certain Keilah participates in the work.
H7084.emploi: Keilah is mentioned 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in 1 Samuel 23 during the episode where David takes refuge there. It is also listed in the census of the cities of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:44) and mentioned in the accounts of post-exilic reconstruction. The name of the city embodies the tension between the refuge offered and potential betrayal, reflecting the political instability of David's time.
H7084.portee: The story of David at Keilah shows the trials of one chosen by God, unjustly pursued and constantly on the run. It teaches the reader that even success and good deeds do not guarantee recognition or safety in this world. It also reminds us of divine providence: David consults God before every decision and receives His answers, revealing that the Lord guides his steps despite apparent dangers.

sens: Mark or design engraved on the skin
Incision made on the body as part of a funerary or religious ritual
H7085.detail:
1. The word refers to a visible mark traced or engraved on the body, particularly on the skin. In Leviticus 19:28, it refers to "figures" that the people of Israel were not to imprint on themselves — distinct, visible signs meant to be noticed.
2. More specifically, it is an incision or mark made in a funerary or mourning context: pagan peoples engraved patterns on their bodies or made cuts to honor their dead or their gods. The Law prohibited this practice for Israel, which implied a certain communion with the dead or idols contrary to faith in the Eternal.
H7085.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the action of engraving, marking, or digging. It is a voluntary action that leaves a lasting, visible trace on the body. The image is that of the work of an engraver or ancient tattoo artist — a thoughtful act that produces a permanent mark.
H7085.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 19:28. It is the only passage that directly addresses this practice among the people of God. The context is clearly legislative: it is a ritual and moral prohibition addressed to the chosen people to distinguish them from the idolatrous practices of neighboring nations. This uniqueness underscores the importance that the Law attaches to this distinction.
H7085.portee: This commandment reminds Christians that the body is to be respected and that certain religious practices — even if they seem sacred elsewhere — are not suitable for the people of God. The believer's body should not be marked by practices that bind to idolatry or deny death as a final reality. It is a call to separation from false worship.

sens: Wide and shallow container for serving food or offerings
Solid silver dish used in the worship of the Tabernacle
H7086.detail:
1. A dish is a wide, open, and shallow container intended to hold and serve food or offerings (Exodus 25:29). It is a table or worship utensil, distinct from cups and chalices, which are deeper and closed.
2. In the context of the Tabernacle and its sacrifices, the dish takes on particular importance: it is a utensil of pure gold or solid silver, heavy and precious, accompanying each grain offering (Numbers 7:19). Filled with fine flour, this dish represents a significant part of the offering consecrated to God.
H7086.origine: The Hebrew word קְעָרָה (qe'arah) designates a wide and flat container. It likely comes from a root that evokes the idea of "digging" or "making hollow," which corresponds to the shape of this utensil. The word belongs to the family of names for cult objects, alongside "cup" (כּוֹס) and "chalice" (כּוֹס). In tradition, this term has been associated with the furnishings of the Tabernacle and the instruments of divine service.
H7086.emploi: This word appears 17 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in passages that describe the furnishings of the Tabernacle (Exodus 25, 37) and the offerings of the leaders of the tribes during the dedication of the Tabernacle (Numbers 7 and 4). Each leader offered a silver dish weighing 130 shekels, filled with fine flour, making it a significant offering. The dish is always associated with other utensils (cups, chalices, bowls) that composed the service of the Tabernacle. Its weight and material (gold or silver) testify to the value and solemnity of its cultic use.
H7086.portee: The dish reminds us that the worship rendered to God in the Old Testament was ordered, material, and concrete: each object had its place, weight, and measure. This precision is not a legalistic quibble, but an expression of our respect for God. Seeing that the tribal leaders brought dishes filled with flour shows that the offering was generous and thoughtful. For Christians, it is an invitation to bring to God not just with the tips of our fingers, but with seriousness and gratitude.

sens: to become thick and compact, referring to a liquid
to solidify or curdle like cheese
to remain still and inactive, referring to people
H7087A.detail:
1. The verb first describes a physical process: a liquid substance becomes thick and dense. In Exodus 15:8, the waters of the sea condense and stand as a solid wall under God's breath — the liquid transforms into something fixed and compact.

2. The image refines with Job 10:10: milk curdles and becomes cheese, a chemical change where the liquid coagulates into solid matter. This is an image of profound and definitive transformation.

3. In Zephaniah 1:12, the verb changes meaning: the men who "rest on their lees" are not physically frozen, but morally numb, immobile in their iniquity. They become "thick," insensitive, closed to God's call — their hearts have condensed into inertia and indifference.
H7087A.origine: The root קפא expresses the fundamental idea of solidification and compactness. It describes what becomes dense, fixed, or immobile. The verb can be used simply (one says that water condenses) or with a direct object to express an action that thickens something (to curdle milk). This same root appears in other Hebrew forms designating what is compact or frozen.
H7087A.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 15:8, it describes a miracle: the waters condense to allow Israel to pass. In Job 10:10, it illustrates the formation of the human body from maternal milk transformed into solid flesh — a biological image of the creative process. In Zephaniah 1:12, it takes on a moral and figurative sense: spiritual indifference resembles a condensation of the heart, a numbness of conscience. The word thus transitions from the physical and tangible domain to the spiritual and metaphorical.
H7087A.portee: This verb invites the believer to perceive how spiritual inertia and indifference can invade the heart, like a substance that thickens and solidifies. In Zephaniah, God's warning targets those who have "condensed" in their security, forgetful of the coming judgment. It is a call to vigilance: one can become insensitive to God without even realizing it, like a liquid that slowly solidifies.

sens: State of low temperature, sensation of cooling
Intensity of cold, winter severity
H7087B.detail:
1. Cold is that state where the temperature drops, where heat decreases. It is the sensation caused by the cooling of air or water. In Zechariah 14:6, on the great day of the Lord, it is said that there will be "no light" but "cold" and ice: the prophet evokes a cosmic transformation where normal light and heat disappear, giving way to cold and frost.
2. The word also designates the intensity of cold, its severity: this quality of what freezes, what indicates solidification by extreme cold. Cold and ice go together in this prophetic passage, like two sides of the absence of heat and life.
H7087B.origine: The Hebrew word קִפָּאוֹן (qippayôn) comes from the root קפא (qp'), which means "to freeze" or "to become frozen." This root evokes the image of liquid solidifying, of water turning into ice under the action of intense cold. The word is formed to designate the state resulting from freezing, the freezing itself, the phenomenon of extreme cold that freezes and solidifies.
H7087B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Zechariah 14:6. The context is highly symbolic and prophetic: it is a picture of cosmic disturbance on the eschatological day of the Lord. Here, "cold" is not simply an ordinary weather condition, but a manifestation of divine judgment or a supernatural transformation of the world. The term is associated with ice and the absence of light, forming a whole that evokes darkness, disorder, and the inversion of the created natural order.
H7087B.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reminds us that God masters the elements of creation: heat, light, cold. On this day of eschatological manifestation, cold symbolizes both judgment and the temporary cessation of familiar order. It is a call to recognize God's sovereignty over all nature and future events.

sens: To slice, to sever cleanly
To abruptly interrupt
To put an end to
To stop in the course of action
H7088.detail:
1. The word primarily means to cut or slice cleanly, as one would with a sharp tool — the image is that of a clean and definitive cut. Isaiah 38:12 uses it to speak of the thread of life that a weaver would cut from his loom: it is the gesture of one who cuts the thread by pulling the loom.
2. By extension, it means to abruptly interrupt the course of something — not just to stop, but to cease in a radical manner. The life of the sick prophet is represented as a weaving interrupted: it is "cut" from the loom, it is finished.
3. The figurative sense refers to ending existence or a situation — here, the imminent death, the human life that is coming to an end. In the context of Isaiah 38, King Hezekiah speaks of his life being cut short by illness.
4. It also means to stop someone in the course of their action or existence before they have finished — to put a final point to what was not completed.
H7088.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of chopping or dividing into pieces. The form used here (Piel) reinforces the action and suggests a clean and intentional cut, not accidental. The central image is that of a clean cut, like that of scissors or a blade that divides in two — hence the link with textile trades where the thread is cut at the loom.
H7088.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 38:12. It is a crucial moment where King Hezekiah, gravely ill and facing death, reflects on his life being taken from him. He uses the language of weavers: his life, like a garment in the process of being made, is brutally cut from the loom. This unique occurrence shows the word in all its emotional weight — not a trivial act, but the definitive, irreversible cut of what could have continued. The context of illness and approaching death gives the verb all its gravity.
H7088.portee: This word speaks to our fragility before God and death. Hezekiah lives in this tension between the inevitable (the cutting death) and hope in God who, ultimately, will heal him. For the believer, this text reminds us that our life is not at our disposal — it is in the hands of the One who can both "cut" and prolong it. It is an invitation to entrust our days to God rather than to appropriate them for ourselves.

sens: Sudden collapse, complete destruction
State of extreme distress and panic in the face of misfortune
H7089.detail:
1. This word designates the total collapse of a city or situation — that which crumbles and disappears. In Ezekiel 7:25, the prophet announces that ruin is coming, that everything is collapsing: it is the image of complete disaster.
2. Beyond material destruction, the word evokes the anguish, the paralyzing terror that seizes one who sees misfortune approaching. It is the panic of shipwreck, the dread of what can no longer be stopped.
H7089.origine: The Hebrew word קְפָדָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of trembling, shivering with fear. It first describes the physical sensation — the shiver of horror — then the inner state of one who is seized by terror. This same root produces the image of shock, of sudden help from calamity.
H7089.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 7:25. The prophet uses it to announce God's judgment on Jerusalem: ruin is coming, people seek it everywhere (salvation), but it is nowhere to be found. It is a moment of absolute crisis where defenses collapse and total terror reigns. This context shows that the word carries both the physical idea of collapse and the psychological experience of disaster.
H7089.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's judgment is not an abstract threat, but a reality that destroys false shelters. It invites seeking true salvation from God rather than relying on walls or earthly riches that crumble.

sens: Small spiny animal that rolls into a ball
Symbol of desolation and ruin
H7090.detail:
1. The hedgehog is a small animal covered with sharp spines, capable of contracting and curling up to protect itself. It is a nocturnal animal that avoids inhabited places. In the Bible, it always appears in contexts of complete destruction and abandonment: Isaiah 14:23 describes a destroyed city that has become the dwelling of the hedgehog, whereas it was once powerful.
2. The hedgehog symbolizes inevitable and irreversible ruin. Its appearance alongside the pelican, the owl, and the raven — all animals of idleness and desolation — marks the fulfillment of divine judgment. Isaiah 34:11 and Zephaniah 2:14 mention it to illustrate that even the most majestic palaces become dens for solitary beasts when God abandons them.
H7090.origine: The Hebrew word קִפֹּד (qippod) literally designates an animal that "contracts" or "curls up" — hence its name in French, derived from the Latin "hericinus." This defensive contraction is characteristic of this animal that rolls into a ball for protection. The word reflects the image of a vulnerable creature that replicates on itself.
H7090.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in prophecies of judgment: twice in Isaiah (chapters 14 and 34) and once in Zephaniah (2:14). In each occurrence, the hedgehog figures among the creatures that will take possession of the ruins of once glorious cities — Babylon, Edom, Nineveh. It is never just an animal; it is a living messenger of desolation, a sign that the place has been completely abandoned to the forces of nature and decline.
H7090.portee: The hedgehog reminds us that human power and the works of pride are fragile before God's justice. Seeing a grand city become the den of this timid and solitary animal expresses the unimaginable extent of the fall. For the believer, it is an invitation not to place trust in visible fortresses, but to fear God, whose judgment completely reshapes kingdoms.

sens: A crawling animal equipped with venomous fangs
H7091.detail: 1. The word here designates a specific reptile: in Isaiah 34:15, amidst the description of a devastated land, this serpent nests and lays its eggs like a bird, suggesting atypical behavior or the poetic use of the word to evoke a particular reptile. The exact meaning of this word remains uncertain: it could refer to a specific snake or an animal that the ancients associated with serpentine behavior.
H7091.origine: The Hebrew word qippoz belongs to a family of words derived from roots evoking rapid movement or rigidity. Its precise etymology remains obscure, but its usage shows that it refers to a well-known creature in the biblical world: the serpent, an emblematic animal of the land of Israel. The term appears only in Isaiah 34:15, making its exact interpretation difficult.
H7091.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 34:15. It is found in a prophetic passage describing Edom (the territory of Esau) after its divine judgment: a desolate land where vegetation disappears and wild animals settle. The serpent represents one of the creatures that will inhabit the human ruins, symbolizing nature reclaiming its rights over a place marked by God's judgment.
H7091.portee: This passage invites the reader to meditate on the consequences of divine judgment: a land once inhabited becomes a den of wild beasts. For the believer, it is a call to take God's warnings seriously and to seek His forgiveness rather than expose oneself to His condemnation.

sens: To close, shut, stop something that is open or flowing
To keep closed, to hold back
To withdraw, to gather oneself (of someone who is dying)
To leap, to jump, to advance by leaps
H7092.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to physically close what is open: to close one's hand (Deuteronomy 15:7), to close the mouth (Job 5:16). The image is one of bringing the two parts of something together to stop it.

2. By extension, it means to refuse, to hold back, to prevent something from manifesting: an iniquity that "closes the mouth" of men, meaning it renders them mute or paralyzes them (Psalms 107:42).

3. In the context of death, the verb describes how a man gathers himself, concentrating to die: one disappears "like all men" (Job 24:24), the body closes in, so to speak, on the death that seizes it.

4. In its participial form, the word evokes a leap or a jump: someone who "leaps" with a quick and rapid movement (Song of Solomon 2:8), an image of movement contrary to closure.
H7092.origine: The verb קָפַץ (qaphats) comes from a root that expresses the idea of tightening, bringing together. In Hebrew, it also has a dimension of sudden movement or contraction. The Qal form (simple) means to close or stop; the Niphal form marks reflexivity (to close in on oneself); the Piel form reinforces the idea of dynamic action, hence the leap or jump which may seem paradoxical but represents a violent and concentrated muscular contraction.
H7092.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in wisdom texts (Job, Psalms) and the Law (Deuteronomy). Its most common usage is in the sense of "to close" or "to hold back": to close one's hand to refuse alms (Deuteronomy 15:7), to close the mouth to remain silent or to be paralyzed by fear or shame (Job 5:16; Psalms 107:42; Isaiah 52:15). In Job 24:24, it describes the moment when a man succumbs to death, closing in on himself. Only one occurrence shows it in the dynamic sense of jumping or leaping (Song of Solomon 2:8), which shows that the verb can express both contraction and the rapid movement resulting from that contraction.
H7092.portee: This word reminds us that God asks us to open our hands and our hearts to the poor: to close one's hand is a refusal to obey (Deuteronomy 15:7). Conversely, when kings "close their mouths" before the Servant of the Lord (Isaiah 52:15), it means they will be silenced by the greatness of what they see — a powerful image of the impact of salvation on the most closed minds.

sens: Point in time when something ends
Spatial extremity, limit of a place or object
Fixed deadline, time by which an act must be accomplished
Final completion of a prophetic or historical period
H7093.detail:
1. The end is the moment when an action, a period, or an existence comes to a close. Cain made his offering "at the end of some time" (Genesis 4:3), meaning after a certain lapse of time has passed. It is the terminal point in the unfolding of time.

2. The end can refer to the physical extremity of something — the end of a region or space. The king visited the cities "at the end" of his lands, marking the extent of his domain.

3. A term is a predetermined temporal limit, like a deadline. The law of the Sabbath commands that "at the end" of seven years there shall be a year of release (Deuteronomy 31:10), a moment determined in advance for what is to happen.

4. The end has an eschatological meaning, that of the final fulfillment of God's purposes. Daniel learns what will happen "at the end of the wrath" (Daniel 8:19), the fulfillment of prophecy in the divine plan. It is also the moment when the life or reign of a person comes to an end: "Our end was approaching, our days were accomplished" (Lamentations 4:18).
H7093.origine: The Hebrew word קֵץ (qets) comes from a root evoking the idea of cutting, slicing — hence the meaning of limiting, setting a boundary. This is why it designates both the end of a duration and the extremity of a space. In Aramaic and in prophetic usage, this word acquires major eschatological significance, describing the completion of the times.
H7093.emploi: This word appears 62 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the books of Daniel, where it takes on a strong prophetic hue. It is first used in a concrete and temporal sense: the end of a fixed period (year of release, seven years, forty days), the end of an action or a life. Gradually, especially among the prophets and in Daniel, it acquires the meaning of eschatological fulfillment — the end of times, the accomplishment of God's plan. In Ezekiel and Daniel, "the end" becomes almost a technical term designating the moment of the final execution of divine judgment. The context determines whether the word remains in the historical time or rises to prophetic meaning.
H7093.portee: This word reminds the reader that everything in this world has an end — every human endeavor, every reign, every life. For the believer in the Old Testament, this means that God controls history, and that the end of times is not chaos but the fulfillment of the divine purpose. By reading the prophets, one understands that the "end" is not an absurd catastrophe, but the moment when God judges and establishes His definitive justice.

sens: To slice, detach a part of an object using a cutting tool
To shear the wool of an animal, to remove its hair by cutting
H7094.detail: 1. The verb denotes the action of cutting, of slicing cleanly. In 2 Kings 6:6, Elisha "cuts" a piece of wood that he throws into the water to make the iron float to the surface — a precise and decisive action. 2. By extension, it means to shear: to remove the wool or hair from an animal using a blade or tool. In Song of Solomon 4:2, the beloved's teeth are compared to "sheared" sheep, smooth and white, coming up from the watering place — the image of regular and radiant beauty.
H7094.origine: The Hebrew verb קָצַב (qatsav) expresses the idea of separating, dividing by a clean cut. Its root evokes the action of the cutting edge. The word belongs to a family of terms related to cutting and separation; it is a concrete verb, rooted in the daily gestures of the ancient world (woodworking, caring for flocks).
H7094.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Kings 6:6, it describes the miraculous act of Elisha cutting wood to make the lost iron float. In the Song of Solomon 4:2, it applies to sheared sheep as a poetic and praising image. The meaning is consistent: an action of separation or removal by cutting, whether material (the wood) or applied to wool (the fleece).
H7094.portee: This simple and concrete word reminds us that God acts in the practical details of human life. The account of Elisha shows that no difficulty escapes His power; the Song invites the believer to see the beauty of the created detail. These two uses testify to the divine presence in the ordinary as well as in the sublime.

sens: The external appearance of a thing, by which its figure is recognized
The extreme point of a thing, its end or base
H7095.detail: 1. This word denotes the visible aspect of an object, what makes its silhouette or recognizable appearance. In Solomon's temple, the two golden cherubim had exactly the same "form": they were identical in their proportions and contours (1 Kings 6:25). It is the idea of a figure that can be seen and remembered. 2. The word can also mean the extremity or base of a thing — the place where it begins or ends. When Jonah speaks of the "roots of the mountains" (Jonah 2:7), he evokes these extreme, deep points, the foundations of the earth that imprisoned him.
H7095.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of shaping, cutting, giving a defined form to something. The Hebrew sees the "form" as the result of an action: one cuts, one shapes, and one obtains a silhouette, a defined contour. That is why the word can also designate the extremity — the place where the material is cut, limited.
H7095.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of precision and measurement. Twice, it describes the architecture of the temple: the ten bases of molten copper were all to have the same "form", just like the two sculpted cherubim. The idea is one of conformity, uniformity in manufacturing. Once, in the book of Jonah, it designates the "roots" — the deep extremity — of the mountains. The context of Jonah 2:7 shows a man in distress, descended to the lowest point, to the foundations of the earth, before being saved.
H7095.portee: This word reminds us that God values order and precision: the temple was to be built with great accuracy, each object having a defined "form". This reflects God's orderly and beautiful thought. For the Christian, it is an invitation to recognize that in the heart of divine service, faithfulness to details matters.

sens: To remove a part of something by slicing or scraping
To reduce, gradually diminish a territory or domain
To cause harm, severely injure someone or something
H7096.detail:
1. The primary meaning is material: to cut, slice, or scrape a surface to remove a part. In Leviticus 14:41, one "scrapes" the inside of a house affected by leprosy to remove the contaminated covering; it is a physical, concrete act necessary for purification. The word evokes the gesture of scraping, removing layer by layer.
2. By extension, "to cut" means to gradually reduce, to trim a territory or possession. In 2 Kings 10:32, the Lord "cuts into" the territory of Israel by the blows inflicted by Hazael: it is a gradual diminishment, piece by piece, as one subtracts from a surface. The image shifts from the knife to territorial loss.
3. In a broader figurative sense, to cut means to destroy or cause severe harm. In Habakkuk 2:10, the tyrant destroys peoples to enlarge his house: the verb denotes the destructive action, the annihilation of what opposes greed. It is to cut short, to end abruptly.
H7096.origine: The Hebrew verb קָצָה (qatsah) belongs to a family of words expressing the action of cutting or removing. Its root evokes the physical gesture of cutting with a cutting instrument (knife, blade). The verb is conjugated in various Hebrew forms: the simple form (Qal) means to cut oneself, the intensive form (Piel) reinforces the action of cutting, and the causative form (Hiphil) expresses the idea of causing to scrape or remove. This word belongs to the vocabulary of concrete action, often related to manual work or destruction.
H7096.emploi: The verb קָצָה appears 5 times in the Old Testament. It is used mainly in the context of ritual purity (Leviticus 14): it involves cleaning a leprous house by scraping its walls. It also appears in contexts of territorial loss or destruction (2 Kings 10:32, Habakkuk 2:10) where it denotes a reduction or annihilation. In Proverbs 26:6, the image of a cut-off foot symbolizes self-sabotage: one who entrusts a message to a fool "cuts off their feet", paralyzing themselves. The word thus oscillates between the material, concrete sense (scraping, cutting) and the figurative sense (reducing, destroying, damaging).
H7096.portee: This verb teaches that destruction or diminishment can be the work of God as punishment (Israel losing its territory) or the result of our own foolish acts (self-sabotage). It also reminds us that purification (removing evil) often involves a difficult and concrete act: sometimes it is necessary to remove, to cut back, to accept a loss in order to be healed. It is a word that calls for vigilance against what harms us, spiritually or materially.

sens: Final point or limit of something — its spatial or temporal end
Edge, border, outline of a region or surface
Mouth of a river or valley
Totality, entirety of something taken in its wholeness
