Temporal expression: at the end of a duration
H7097A.detail:
1. The extremity is the point or limit that marks the end of something. In Judges 6:21, the angel advances the extremity of the staff he holds to touch the meat and the bread: it is the end of the staff, its terminal point. This applies to any physical length.
2. The word also designates the edge or border of a region, its outer limit. In Numbers 22:36, Balak goes out to meet Balaam at the limit (extremity) of the Arnon, the river that marks the border.
3. At the mouth of a watercourse or valley, extremity names the point where the river joins a larger body of water. The geographical context of the passages indicates this precise meaning.
4. By condensation of language, extremity can mean the totality of something: what is understood between two extremities. Thus, in Isaiah 42:10, singing "to the extremities of the earth" means singing in every corner of the world, everywhere on the entire earth.
5. In a temporal expression, extremity means "at the end of" a duration: in 2 Kings 8:3, "at the end of seven years," it means after seven full years.
H7097A.origine: The Hebrew word qatseh (קָצֶה) comes from a root that expresses the idea of cutting, delimiting, setting a limit. This root evokes the action of determining a point beyond which one does not go. The word is related to verbs meaning "to cut," "to trim," or "to impose a limit": the extremity is what "cuts" continuity, what "stops." The same root generates other words in the family designating limitation or end.
H7097A.emploi: The word appears 83 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the historical books (Numbers, Joshua, Kings) and the prophets. It is very frequent in the geographical descriptions of the borders of the territories of Israel, where it precisely delineates the boundaries of the lands assigned to each tribe. It is also found in travel narratives and delays ("at the end of so many days"). The Segond translates it mainly as "extremity," "end," and "border." From context to context, the word oscillates between the physical and geometric idea of the "final point" and the broader idea of "totality" or "whole": thus, "the extremities of the earth" does not designate precise points but the whole earth without exception.
H7097A.portee: Understanding "extremity" helps the biblical reader grasp the precision of divine language: God speaks in terms of limits, borders, fulfillment. When Scripture marks an end — a border, a duration elapsed, a geographical limit — it affirms the order of the created world: everything has its boundaries, everything comes to an end. This strengthens faith: God masters the limits. This notion also illuminates how the Old Testament delineates space and time: through precise delimitation, reflecting a worldview where everything has its rightful place.

sens: Point where something stops or disappears
Moment when life ends
Abundance so great that it seems limitless
H7097B.detail:
1. The end is the terminal point of something: where it takes an end, where it stops. In Isaiah 2:7, treasures are "without end," meaning that one cannot see where they stop, so abundant they are. It is the natural culmination of a reality, what bounds or terminates.
2. The end can designate death, the cessation of life. In Nahum 3:3, the "dead" to infinity is an absolute, tragic end: the last moment when life turns.
3. By extension, "end" expresses a quantity or power without limit, a staggering abundance. In Nahum 2:10 and 3:9, "without end" and "innumerable" describe a wealth or strength so immense that one cannot fix its term: they seem infinite.
H7097B.origine: The word קֵצֶה (qétsé) is a variant of the word קָצֶה (qatsé), both derived from a root meaning "to cut, to slice." The basic image is that of a cut, a separation: the end of something is where it is "cut off," where it stops. This root belongs to a family of Hebrew words evoking cessation, extremity, limit.
H7097B.emploi: The word appears four times in the provided texts, all in the prophets (Isaiah and Nahum). In each occurrence, it designates a cessation or a limit. In Isaiah 2:7, it is used to qualify wealth without term. In Nahum 2:10 and 3:3, it describes either treasures or a death without measure, in a context of catastrophe. In Nahum 3:9, the context of innumerable strength recalls the idea of a quantity that cannot be bounded. The word colors the idea of unlimitedness, infinity, often linked to abundance or destruction.
H7097B.portee: Understanding the word "end" helps the reader grasp how Scripture speaks of limits and infinity. When the Bible says that a good or a judgment is "without end," it expresses a reality that surpasses human measure and strikes the mind. It is a word that reminds us that everything created has an end — except what touches the eternity of God and the lasting consequences of His acts.

sens: Physical limit of an object, surface, or expanse
Terminal point or end of something
Part included in a whole, taken from the totality
H7098.detail:
1. The extremity is the physical limit at both ends of an object: the two golden cherubim are placed "at the two extremities of the mercy seat" (Exodus 25:18), just as the rings are fixed "at the two extremities of the breastplate" (Exodus 28:23). It is the point where a surface or a three-dimensional object ends.
2. The word also designates the far limits of a large expanse: God "created the extremities of the earth" (Isaiah 40:28), meaning the most distant regions, the borders of the habitable world.
3. In a less common but present sense in the Bible, the word can mean "among," "from the midst of": when it says "priests taken from all the people" (1 Kings 13:33), the extremity designates what is included in the whole, a part drawn from the total.
H7098.origine: The Hebrew word qatsah comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to determine a limit." It expresses the idea of marking an end, of delimiting. The family of the word includes terms related to cutting and separation. In Greek, this word is generally rendered by "péras" (limit) or "akron" (summit, extremity).
H7098.emploi: This word appears about 30 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Pentateuch (notably Exodus with the details of the Tabernacle) and the prophets. In the context of worship (Exodus), it designates the extreme points of sacred objects — the sides of the Ark of the Covenant, the rings of the priestly breastplate. In biblical poetry (Isaiah, Psalms), it expands to a cosmic scope: the extremities of the earth evoke the immensity of divine creation. The word slightly shifts in nuance depending on whether it concerns concrete and delimited objects or infinite spaces.
H7098.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the creative action and divine sovereignty: God does not tire in creating "the extremities of the earth," which reminds us of His omniscience and limitless power. In the worship of the Tabernacle, the extremity is also a point of junction: it is where sacred elements meet, reminding us that God is at the limits of our understanding, yet accessible through ordered worship.

sens: Edge or farthest point of an expanse
Boundary of a territory or space
End or terminal point of a distance
H7099.detail:
1. The word designates the end or the farthest place of a region: "Your praise reaches to the extremities of the earth" (Psalms 48:11) means that God's glory reaches the most remote confines, the farthest points of the known world.
2. It also signifies the limit or boundary of a country or region: "You have enlarged the borders of the land" (Isaiah 26:15) speaks of the boundaries that are pushed back to enlarge the territory.
3. More generally, it is the end or edge of any distance: the extremity is the point where something ends or where another space begins.
H7099.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to cut" or "to sever." An extremity is where something is "cut off," where it stops. The Hebrew word is related to the idea of separation and delimitation: it marks the end of one thing and the beginning of another.
H7099.emploi: The word is used three times in the Hebrew Bible. It first appears in poetry with the meaning of "extremities of the earth" to designate the farthest and most remote regions of the world (Psalms 48:11 and 65:6), often to express the universality of divine power or glory. It is also used in Isaiah 26:15 to speak of the limits or boundaries of a territory, with a nuance of progression or enlargement.
H7099.portee: This word reminds us that God reigns over the entire universe, even in its most distant and least known parts. For the believer, this means that divine power and grace have no boundaries and reach all peoples, without exception.
